Our in-depth examination of highly energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into two segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns aligns with the structure of the local intergalactic medium. The absence of similar anisotropy patterns in lower energy groups suggests a critical energy threshold for the observed patterns, potentially linked to the presence of nearby sources or specific cosmic-ray particle trajectories. Our findings underscore the complex and nuanced nature of high-energy cosmic-ray phenomena. The widespread distribution of these anisotropy patterns across the sky further supports the notion that nearby sources, within the order of tens of Mpc, may account for a substantial portion of the high-energy cosmic ray stream. The precise spatial configuration of these sources, however, remains unclear and warrants further investigation. The observed patterns of energy-dependent anisotropy and their relationship to the local intergalactic medium also raise important questions about the underlying mechanisms that shape the high-energy cosmic ray stream. The extensive coverage and detailed energy and direction resolution of the Pierre Auger Observatory have made it possible to detect similar patterns of anisotropy in highly energetic cosmic rays at even higher energy levels, up to 72 EeV, through the application of advanced statistical methods. These more inclusive analyses identified patterns of quadrupolar and hexapolar modulation in the most energetic group, but they require confirmation with an expanded and more sophisticated dataset. The study of these anisotropy patterns and their evolution with rising energy levels offer valuable insights into the origins of high-energy cosmic rays. The vast scope of the Pierre Auger Observatory has made it possible to study the spatial distribution of these sources and the cosmic ray stream on a large scale, extending far beyond the immediate vicinity of the most energetic cosmic ray event recorded to date. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, our framework and its applications surpass previous works, with no additional conditions necessary to ensure the validity of our results.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose that matches the descriptors from the NDF to known training
examples, prior to executing the task. NDFs are efficiently trained without the
need for explicit pose estimation components, and successfully generalize to novel
object instances and poses, as shown through manipulation tasks on the MOANA
dataset. With 13 out of 16 categories successfully repeating tasks on novel
instances, our method significantly outperforms existing alternatives. Code is available at: https://github.com/ethan-choi/neural-descriptor-fields.

estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. The method in question is publicly accessible through the Open Source MolSchemas project.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This algorithm first solves a system of equations based on the dependence between layers and then uses a modification of the traditional Power Iteration Method to find the centrality values. We also establish the convergence of this algorithm and demonstrate its applicability to problem scenarios. Furthermore, our method provides a concise and intuitive interpretation of the centrality values in multi-layered networks. Lastly, our method has a linear complexity when comparing the calculation of centrality values to the size of the network, making it an efficient approach for tackling large-scale network problems. We validate our method by applying it to a real-world mobile phone data set, demonstrating its capability to identify hidden communities across different layers. This approach is suitable for a broad range of applications involving complex, multi-aspect networks. The code associated with this research is publicly accessible on GitHub. During this surface seal process, a partial seal forms around the sphere, and it eventually merges with the water body beneath. This phenomenon was observed in a laboratory setting, with high-speed cameras capturing the water entry process for spheres of various sizes, moving at a range of speeds. The results show that the surface seal process is influenced by both the sphere's size and the force of its impact, and it can be broken down into distinct stages. Furthermore, the study reveals that the speed at which the water rushes upwards to meet the incoming sphere plays a significant role in shaping the surface seal and determines whether the water and sphere eventually combine smoothly or result in a splashing or spattering effect. The findings from this research were then incorporated into an existing model of the water entry process, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the surface seal and paving the way for related improvements. The study's outcomes also highlight the complexities of the water entry process and the challenges associated with developing simple, universally applicable models. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories, allowing for the breaking of global Yang-Mills symmetries, extending the scope of $\theta$-terms to also include non-gauge groups such as $E_8$, $F_4$, and $G_2$. When coupled to a Kalb-Ramond field, they also lead to the breaking of the Lorentzian group $SO(1,3)$ to $SO(3)$. Generalized $\theta$-terms prove particularly well-suited for describing the results of non-perturbative effects caused by D7-branes in a way that is both physically equivalent and computationally more straightforward. Moreover, they highlight the distinct, physically distinguishable phases of the theory existing as a result of non-perturbative effects caused by D7-branes. Finally, we explored the possibility of the $\Omega$-orientation of D7-branes giving rise to an $\theta$-term for the non-gauge group $Spin(7)$, discovering it is both physically and conceptually meaningful. The case of the $\theta$-term for $Spin(7)$ also yields a novel, non-perturbative, physically distinct phase of the theory existing as a result of D7-branes. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. By exploring different phases, our results show that cubanite's unique properties depend on it being half-metallic, with ferromagnetism arising directly from the orbital selectivity and localized nature of the electrons. This has implications for the little-studied iron sulfide family and offers a specific case of orbital selectivity. In cubanite, it manifests as the geometric arrangement of electrons in space, with $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals configured in a specific way that cannot be achieved in simpler compounds like magnetite. This unique arrangement gives cubanite its anomalous magnetic and electronic properties, setting it apart from other compounds with similar electronic configurations but different geometric arrangements of their electrons. This discovery provides a theoretical explanation for the compound's unusual magnetic and electronic behavior and could be relevant to other sulfide compounds with similar configurations. This work also highlights the potential uses of cubanite in advanced technologies that utilize specific magnetic and electronic properties. This compound's unique behavior has not been observed in any other compounds with the same electron configuration, making it an isolated case that could be referred to as "orbital chauvinism". This phenomenon is so rare that it may only occur in this particular compound, but it could also provide a general principle that applies to other compounds with the same configuration but a different geometric arrangement of their electrons. This discovery challenges the current understanding of how electrons behave in compounds and could lead to a deeper understanding of how they interact with each other and their surroundings. This may also have implications for the origin of Earth's magnetic field and could provide a connection between this compound and other iron-rich compounds that give off geological heat. This could be related to the Earth's core, which is composed of iron and nickel, and may give insight into how the Earth's heat and magnetic field are generated and sustained. This could also give a theoretical basis for the compounds that make up the Earth's core and provide a framework for understanding the compounds that give off the heat and energy needed to maintain the Earth's magnetic field and keep it rotating. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. The proposed system, with its dark excitons and external driving field, has been theoretically demonstrated to exhibit phonon-burst emission of various sizes, thereby offering a practical solution for phonon-gun technology. We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we created a model from coupled, 1D, Peierl's Hamiltonians and discovered that the low-energy physics of this model is identical to that of the original, 2D, herringbone lattice. Lastly, we analyzed a phase with a spatially-modulated, superconducting phase transition and found that the low-energy physics can be described using a lattice version of the Shakya-Shastry model. This model contains only three nearest-neighbor, in-phase, hopping terms and exhibits non-interacting, fermionic degrees of freedom within the immediate vicinity of the critical point. This finding is distinct from the well-known, exactly-solved, Heisenberg and Shastry-Shakya models that only contain four- and three-neighbor, out-of-phase, hopping terms, respectively. This new model also exhibits a type of mass gap that arises from the interaction between the onsite, electronic interaction and the lattice structure. This interaction becomes a true, zero-mass, Goldstone fermion only at the high-symmetry points within the first Brillouin zone along the reciprocal lattice vector. This feature is distinct from the massless, Drude-like behavior exhibited by the Heisenberg and Shastry-Shakya models along their respective reciprocal lattice vectors. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. We also explore the feasibility of creating these states in optical parametric oscillators, finding that they can generate SPCCSs when operating within a specific frequency range, and offer a practical method for converting these states to other non-classical states. Lastly, we discuss the potential applications of SPCCSs in quantum information processing and outline a strategy for extending this research to other types of states.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information in the form of previous cancer history, radiology reports, and endoscopic data. However, there is no standardized method for incorporating this additional information into the segmentation process. In this study, we incorporated both radiological reports and previous cancer history into the segmentation process, ignoring the spatial structure of the esophagus. We developed a novel artificial neural network called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which effectively incorporates external information by assigning different importance levels to specific features. The DDAUnet architecture comprises two main components: a residual block and a dense attention module. It employs external information to create a dense mask that affects feature integration levels across the network. The developed model was tested using a limited dataset, and the results showed improved performance compared to standard Unet architecture and other state-of-the-art models. The DDAUnet has the potential to be trained on large datasets that incorporate external information, making it suitable for a wide range of image segmentation tasks. The code for the DDAUnet model has been made publicly available on GitHub. The limited esophageal tumor dataset used in this research is also available for public use after obtaining the necessary permissions. The results of this research have been presented at the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. The DDAUnet model achieved outstanding performance in the segmentation of abnormal lung tissue in CT scans, surpassing the performance of 12 other state-of-the-art models. The developed model also successfully integrated external information in the form of radiology reports, assigning different levels of importance to specific features. The DDAUnet consists of a dense attention module that creates a mask to control feature integration levels across the network, and it can be trained using a large dataset that incorporates external information, making it suitable for a wide range of image segmentation tasks. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. By doing so, we highlight opportunities to create more inclusive technologies benefiting diverse societal groups.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique nematic properties exhibited by Ta atoms in some structures, however the oxide's fundamental crystal form is disputed as it has been reported in five different space groups. Using Monte Carlo simulations in conjunction with direct space structural optimization, we investigated the potential ground state structures of Ta$_2$O$_5$ to determine the most stable configurations and differentiate between the reported space groups, ultimately suggesting that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s ground state structure is Cc, not previously confirmed through experimental means.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Ultimately, successful strategies for curtailing the spread of misinformation must address these underlying societal elements. Additionally, we highlight avenues for further research into the influential role of Big Sort on election-related information dissemination and covert propaganda. The underlying principles of this study may also be applicable to similar phenomena in other countries. The empirical data underlying this research is available for public use. The findings of this research were previously presented at the Annual Meeting of the National Communication Association in 2020. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. The research provides a foundation for using human speech in robotic learning and suggests possible applications in providing more accurate robotic performance by learning from previously demonstrated tasks. The underlying model of human speech during robotic instruction can be further improved to increase the efficacy of this approach. The data and model used in this study consist of 30 separate manipulation instruction demonstrations performed by five different individuals. The research was conducted in a controlled environment using a small sample size, and future work could benefit from scaling to a larger sample size and more complex task settings. The findings have implications for using human speech in other robotic learning methods, such as through imitation learning, and provide a foundation for incorporating audio feedback into robotic teaching systems via speech input. The model of human speech during robotic instruction also has value in its own right as a standalone model of human speech, without any necessary connection to robotic learning. The data used in this research is available for public use. The model of human speech during robotic instruction was developed using a general-purpose language model without any modifications, and the research provides a novel application for this model of human speech. The model consists of a combination of a vocabulary model and a set of hidden Markov models, and the research provides a novel interpretation of the structure of this model. The data used in this research consists of audio files in WAV format with a sampling rate of 16 kHz and speech files in FLAC format with a sampling rate of 48 kHz, and the speech was analyzed using a set of 39 features commonly used in deep learning models. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. This work was presented at the ACM SIGSOFT 21.39 and arXiv:2111.13018.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significance as data is frequently dispersed across distinct platforms. Multiple sparse domains with interconnected yet distinct attributes pose a particular challenge. In this paper, a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) is introduced to address this issue. MSDCR builds upon the foundation of Aspect Preference Learning (APL) and incorporates a dual-enhanced approach to capture intricate connections within multi-sparse domains. This involves employing an Inter-Domain Aspect Preference Learning (IDAPL) module to integrate cross-domain attributes and an Intra-Domain Aspect Preference Learning (IDAPL) module to explore the internal structure of each individual domain. IDAPL is further subdivided into two tiers: a first tier that detects explicit intra-domain attributes and a second tier that discovers implicit aspects via negative sampling. By accounting for both inter- and intra-domain aspects, MSDCR generates a comprehensive preference profile for recommendation. The efficacy of MSDCR is illustrated through experimental results on multiple sparse domains, demonstrating its superiority over existing cross-domain and APL methods. Moreover, MSDCR's versatility is established by successful application to multi-sparse domain recommendation in real-world scenarios. The code for MSDCR is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/TextMask/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The release of Hypatia is accompanied by an interactive web tool enabling the creation of reduced conic formulations from existing ones. The project source code is also made available on GitHub under the MIT open-source license. The accompanying web-based tool can be accessed at www.hypatia.dev. The package is currently available for Julia and will be developed further with the aim of expanding it to include a C++ interface in the future. The proposed method has the potential to be used with a wide range of interior-point solvers, including but not limited to GDOF. The release of Hypatia marks an advancement in the field of interior-point methods and provides a valuable tool for practitioners relying on complex conic formulations. The method also has the potential to discover previously unknown reduced conic formulations. The development of Hypatia was funded by the Australian Research Council. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further examination was conducted to address which preprocessing steps are crucial for imaging features extracted from MRIQC. This study also explored two approaches for training models on small, representative samples for scaling up to larger datasets. Finally, our findings were applied to simplify the MRIQC pipeline, removing preprocessing steps that do not significantly impact the results. This research was presented at the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention in 2019.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. A dual decomposition was utilized to solve this complex problem efficiently. A case study was conducted in Los Angeles to demonstrate the practical applications of this model, with multiple scenarios explored to analyze the effects of private EVs on grid recovery. Our findings reveal that private EVs can reduce congestion, lower emissions, and both decrease and increase grid recovery costs depending on the distance between transportation routes and the grid, with longer routes generally leading to higher recovery costs. A notable outcome of this research is the discovery that private EVs may become "obstacles" to sustainable transportation by exacerbating grid recovery costs in certain urban environments. A potential mitigation strategy proposed here involves offering incentives to private EV owners to use specific routes that minimize grid recovery costs. A numerical analysis was also performed to assess the financial implications of providing such incentives to private EV owners. A discussion on how this research can be further improved by incorporating elements of game theory and uncertainties in transportation and energy systems is presented. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Consequently, this research provides the first instance of a rendezvous scenario characterized by a strange attractor within the Motivation Dynamics framework, and our findings also reveal that this scenario is marked by unequal meeting frequencies between the agents, with one dominating the encounters. Furthermore, we identify a critical threshold that must be surpassed for a stable, long-term rendezvous to occur. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, our findings suggest that intermetallic GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds exhibit excellent mechanical strength, making them suitable for high-pressure studies. Lastly, our calculations predict that the A-type anti-ferromagnetic and metallic characteristics can be retained by doping GdSn3 with up to 75% Cm content. Lastly, we propose that intermetallic GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds, exhibiting both magnetic properties and mechanical strength, may be valuable for pressure sensors in spintronics.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we propose a new parameter that combines the effects of lensing and the inherent scatter in SN Ia progenitors and is calculable from $\rho(r)$ and the mean mass of SN Ia white dwarf companions. This new parameter exhibits a narrower dispersion when compared to standard models of galactic haloes and may be a more precise indicator of the underlying physics driving SN Ia explosions. Additionally, we explored the potential for lensing to influence the observed peak brightness of SNe Ia but found no detectable correlation. As such, the primary contribution of this research lies in providing a non-cosmological explanation for the scatter present in SN Ia data and highlighting the importance of considering lensing effects in future analyses. Given the limited resolution of current SN Ia samples, we anticipate a significantly stronger signal for lensing in upcoming datasets with improved resolution. As such, we propose an straightforward method for calculating the lensing parameter from SN Ia data using a simple and widely accepted model of galactic haloes and suggest future research employing deep weak lensing maps derived from SN Ia photometry. Given the overlap in the types of galaxies affected by lensing and those useful as SN Ia cosmology probes, we propose an alternative method for selecting SN Ia samples based on the presence or absence of lensing effects. As such, this approach may help mitigate the impact of foreground lensing on certain analyses involving the SDSS and similar surveys. Given the limited scope of this analysis, we emphasize the potential for further insights into the dynamics of SN Ia explosions and the properties of galactic haloes surrounding their progenitors. As such, we encourage researchers with access to deep lensing maps and SN Ia data to explore this issue in greater detail. Given the relatively simple method employed in this research, such an analysis would primarily require access to sufficient computational resources. Given the limited duration of this project, we were unable to perform any such analysis.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has progressed, there are still many unknowns about their behavior, which has been compounded by the lack of a unified model explaining their optical activity. This review aims to provide an in-depth examination of the static and dynamic electrical control methods that have been employed to manage T centers, as well as offer a comprehensive picture of the defect's physical makeup based on prior studies. We also outline the types of T centers that are likely to exist and discuss the implications of these findings for quantum technology applications. Moreover, we highlight the importance of further computational modeling to gain a deeper understanding of the silicon T center and identify areas where experimental progress has already been made. As such, this review is intended to be beneficial not just to newcomers to the field but also to seasoned researchers who can use this information to guide their own experimental and theoretical pursuits.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given text dataset. Specifically, we analyze the effect of word frequencies and semantic relationships on the dimensions used in the model's representation. To this end, we leverage measures from linear algebra, information theory, and probability. Our findings reveal that the efficacy of word embeddings is closely tied to the presence of a normal distribution in the bag-of-words data. We also develop a theoretical framework that can be used to guide future applications of the model, including the skip-gram architecture. Furthermore, we experimentally validate our findings by assessing the quality of the model through both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations. Our results demonstrate a noticeable improvement in performance when imposing a Gaussian distribution constraint on the data, thereby supporting our theoretical model. We also explore the implications of our work for other word embeddings models, revealing that many share similar structures and are therefore likely susceptible to the same issues. We conclude by examining the potential pitfalls and solutions for the common problems encountered with these models, and suggest a promising alternative called the Gaussian Embedding Model. This model outperforms the skip-gram architecture in both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations, and is available for public use. We end by considering the widespread adoption of these models and the lack of rigorous mathematical analysis that underpins this phenomenon. We believe that the models' widespread adoption is largely attributable to their simplicity and ease of implementation, and that they have become "magical black boxes" with an air of mystique surrounding them. We hope that this paper will help to dispel this mystique and provide a deeper understanding of these models, as well as offering practical advice for their use. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research builds upon the preceding work presented at the AISTATS conference in 2021.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, effectively 
incorporating various references. Our research spans multiple text generation 
tasks at various levels of conversational depth. Ultimately, our primary model, 
known as Harvest, showcases superior performance in responding accurately in 
conversational settings. Notably, Harvest excels in a straightforward text 
generation task. Our investigation of Harvest through the MultiTalk Dataset 
reveals a dense, intricate response distribution that underlies its functioning. 
Furthermore, Harvest distinguishes itself as a pioneering use of text 
 manipulation. Our findings related to Harvest yield actionable improvement 
guidelines. Our research, coupled with the vast MultiTalk Dataset, paves the 
way for tackling various diverse text generation tasks. Lastly, we outline a 
simple dialogue generation model incorporating Harvest as our base model, 
which, when combined with a reinforcement learning-based module, learns to select 
the most appropriate response from numerous possibilities. This model, in turn, 
evolves into a more sophisticated controller that effectively crafts novel text 
branches. Our code as well as the MultiTalk Dataset are publicly accessible.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is available for download at [www.website.com].

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. Conversely, we derive the Dyson and Bru-Wishart processes as local statistics for multiple SLE on the real line and the positive reals, respectively. Notably, these results specialize to the initial findings of Miller and Sheffield for the upper half-plane and provide novel extensions to the first orthant of the complex plane. Additionally, they establish the equivalence between whole-line SLE driven by the Dyson model and the Bru-Wishart process and the statistics of geodesics in the Tyran-Kaminski-Hulri model. Lastly, we obtain the whole-line SLE driven by the Airy process as a specific instance of this framework.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, by integrating insights from regulatory elements with SNPs, we have modeled population specific trait variation due to changes in genome-wide accessibility with an estimated 30% contribution in several cases. Lastly, by categorizing SNPs into distinct cellular control mechanisms with an estimated 20% contribution in several cases, our study provides a comprehensive framework for interpreting and understanding the complex interplay between genomics and trait variation. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it uses Natural Language Inference (NLI) to supplement the semantic similarity task, enhancing the capability to capture response diversity's underpinning logic. Secondly, an end-to-end neural model is proposed, incorporating a dual-objective loss function with a contrastive NLI loss and a contrastive semantic loss to generate responses with greater diversity while adhering to the input constraints. Evaluations, in the form of novel semantic similarity and natural language understanding assessments, confirm the model's effectiveness in producing more diverse responses. Furthermore, a conversation duration experiment validates the practical benefits of this model in real-world conversations. The model's source code is available at https://github.com/ghruvoi/Diversity_NLI.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins too fast and breaks apart, taking approximately 10-30 years to occur once it reaches this state. The modeling of the latter scenario resulted in a formula for the time it takes to the star loses mass, with an expression involving the angular momentum, magnetic field, and surface temperature. This led to the prediction of the surface temperature over time in the latter scenario. The computer simulations also accounted for external forces caused by gravitational contraction and opacities caused by electron degeneracy in highly compressed matter. The modeling showed that matter compression does not significantly impact the boundaries of hydrogen burning. The computer simulations were validated by comparing the results with existing observations of white dwarfs and low-mass stars. The occurrence of hydrogen burning in low-mass stars also depends on their metal content, with a decrease in the mass limit for hydrogen burning with an increase in metal content. The research paper then explored the possible outcomes for sub-stellar objects with masses between 0.1 and 0.5 solar masses, with a focus on objects with surface temperatures less than 3000K. The computer simulations showed that these objects experience significant contraction due to electron degeneracy pressure, rather than gravitational contraction, with the resulting matter compression leading to diverse outcomes, including the breaking apart, massive accretion of material, or extreme spinning caused by gravitational contraction. The computer simulations also showed that the surface temperature of these objects decreases with time, rather than remaining constant, with the rate of this decrease controlled by the angular momentum rather than the spin-down time. The research paper then applied the computer simulations to validate the existence of cool low-mass sub-stellar objects, with a predicted population of 10 to the power of 9

The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. Finally, the BigApple parameter set is utilized to investigate neutron star binaries' gravitational wave signals, specifically the canonical love number, tidal radius, and moment of inertia, which are crucial for interpreting future observations and improving the understanding of dense matter. The BigApple energy density functional provides a solid foundation for investigating neutron star matter's composition and comptonization in neutron star binaries. Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. Experimentally verifying its predicted properties through magnetization, X-ray absorption, and bulk measurements can help advance an understanding of theoretical models and provide a practical application for $sp^{2}$-electron based materials in solid state physics.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be refined to a high degree of precision, and with existing data, a more stringent limit can be set with certain heavy neutral particle masses. Furthermore, with a more sensitive photon veto system, NA62 could set even tighter limits on the heavy neutral particle's interaction with the heavy electron sector. Additionally, this research highlighted the significance of improving the photon veto's trigger system to discover heavy neutral particles in the experiment. With optimized detection methods, NA62 can either discover heavy neutral particles or set an even lower limit on their interaction with the heavy electron sector. Based on different detection methods, restrictions on heavy neutral particle interactions can be $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-8}$, and this capability will be realized through the NA62 experiment's analysis of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach demonstrates notable success in reconstructing three-dimensional faces from images depicting large head orientations, with face reconstruction success rates exceeding 90% in scenarios with moderate head orientations and exceeding 80% in scenarios with extreme head orientations. The improved results achieved with our technique indicate that modeling both head orientation and occlusion is crucial for achieving highly accurate three-dimensional face reconstruction. Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes. They also computed exact values for this average in certain specific cases. Further, they identified connections to enumerative structures known as rational functions with negative coefficients. Lastly, they connected the problem to a compound process involving the number of steps in a random walk that stays non-negative, ultimately reaching the highest peak. This peak itself can be seen as the number of deepest nodes in a corresponding marked ordered tree. This walk-based interpretation allows for calculation of the probability that the most inner node is located at a particular distance from the root. This, in turn, enables derivation of the generating function for the number of deepest nodes, and hence for marked ordered trees. This final generating function can also be obtained directly from first principles. The research mentioned has been previously published in the journal Advances in Applied Mathematics, volume 83. In recent years, significant progress made in large-scale data processing capabilities has led to the increased use of linear models with a vast number of parameters being estimated from large datasets. This over-parametrization enables these models to achieve excellent performance. However, research in this field is hampered by the existing statistical theory, which cannot accommodate models with an excessive number of parameters. This paper addresses this limitation by developing a non-asymptotic learning theory for over-parameterized linear models in time series data. It establishes a bound on the estimation error and provides a reconstruction algorithm with a guarantee of successfully recovering the underlying structure. Furthermore, it demonstrates that there is a range of models with increasing numbers of parameters where recovery is still possible. In addition, we analyze a specific scenario with a random covariance matrix and derive precise estimates for the overhead required for recovery. This is shown to scale polynomially with key characteristics of the data, in particular, the dimensionality, the time series length, and the eigenvalue spectrum of the covariance matrix. This is a significant advancement over the existing asymptotic bounds discussed in the literature. This research was motivated by the desirability to develop a robust linear predictive model for a wide range of applications involving time series data. It provides a starting point for this purpose by establishing a foundation on which more sophisticated models, with additional features like regularization and resampling, can be built. It also offers insights that can be used to design such models and provides a framework for evaluating their performance in a statistically rigorous manner. It is worth noting that the terms over-parametrization, overfitting, and benign overfitting are used interchangeably in this paper. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal that successful implementation of storage relies heavily on clever scheduling techniques. Currently, the prevailing approach relies on large, sophisticated batteries being operated by utility companies. In contrast, a growing number of behind-the-meter installations are being managed by various private entities, including individuals, with different risk-taking attitudes. Existing research primarily focuses on optimizing storage operations with an eye on minimizing costs or capitalizing on market opportunities, but often disregards the impact of uncertain market behavior. Furthermore, most models fail to account for the varying risk profiles of private parties. This study addresses these limitations by developing a robust self-scheduling model for storage operators willing to participate in competitive markets with price and generation uncertainty. By employing robust optimization, the model effectively mitigates the effects of market unpredictability and incorporates risk aversion into decision-making. The proposed approach also takes into consideration various storage technologies with distinct risk preferences and different cost structures. A numerical study utilizing real-world data from the Australian electricity market validates the effectiveness of the model. The resulting framework provides valuable insights for private parties, energy management companies, and utility companies seeking to operate storage in competitive electricity markets. Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a computational model of two-electron behavior has been created by applying a configuration interaction approach based on a multi-valley effective mass theory. By utilizing the same experimental parameters, a comprehensive set of positions, with up to several nanometers of separation, has been calculated for the hyperfine-signal amplitude in silicon fin structures, including both individual donors and those with exchange-coupling. Additionally, the effective two-qubit gate fidelity as a function of distance between qubits has been determined, providing valuable insights for placement of qubits within finite-width fins without compromising the functionality of the two-qubit gate. Existing data, including hyperfine-sensitive reflectometry measurements, have been utilized to develop a precise validation of the model. A user-friendly application has been created to guide users through inputting experimental parameters and calculating corresponding data, facilitating further development of silicon-based quantum processors.

Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed to explain these findings. This model highlights the significance of a specific alignment of the Fermi level within the quantum well's energy spectrum for reducing resistance oscillations. Both experimental and theoretical results presented here contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the unique properties exhibited by HgTe quantum wells and highlight the importance of precise control over the Fermi level within these systems. This has implications for developing devices that utilize edge states and provide resistance modulation. Additionally, this work paves the way for examining interactions between edge and bulk states in other two-dimensional systems with a direct or indirect energy spectrum. This could potentially reveal new ways of modulating interactions and enhancing the coherence of edge states and other systems with a neutral point. This has been achieved by examining transport properties across small-sized samples with a controlled amount of disorder and temperature. This has allowed for the examination of interaction between the edge and bulk states and examining the effects of this interaction on the formation of the reservoir mentioned earlier. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, simulations in an indoor scenario with fewer but more densely packed small cells highlight the importance of proper choice of the cell penetration loss parameter in modeling cellular interference. Furthermore, we investigated how our solution handles imprecise local estimates of power allocation. Lastly, we explored the impact of our solution's key parameters on performance.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively reduces the spread of incorrect predictions and boosts the model's accuracy. Furthermore, the framework is versatile and can be applied in real-world settings, such as developing more reliable models for navigating self-driving cars. We also explore a more advanced version of the framework, extending the model's pipeline with a machine learning model that incorporates the refined data through reinforcement learning, which in turn refines the model's performance. This advanced version, in turn, can be viewed as a specialized implementation of the proposed collaborative learning framework, which we have dubbed "cleanplay." The term "cleanplay" captures the essence of this collaborative approach, which requires both human and machine components to adhere to straightforward, clearly defined rules of engagement in order to develop more effective and reliable models quickly. We have put the "cleanplay" version of the framework through testing and found it to be an highly efficient method for resolving situations that involve deceptive data. The proposed framework, along with the "cleanplay" variant, has been made available on GitHub for public use. The results of our testing are also available in the form of animated visualizations. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Lastly, we establish a relationship between $J_n^T$ and the truncated colored volume conjecture.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  A subsequent evaluation of a gold-standard dataset featuring latent sense annotations yields promising findings, with 57.3% of instances achieving perfect sense accuracy when employing BERT and 62.9% when combining BERT with hypernyms' definitions.  A subsequent investigation into the efficacy of context-gloss augmentation in addressing latent WSD tasks by randomly reducing the Senses Per Word (SPW) yields notable performance gains, with an average 10% F1-score increase when employing BERT and 15% when combining BERT with hypernyms' definitions.  A subsequent analysis of task difficulty is conducted by categorizing words into three distinct groups based on SPW, revealing a linear positive correlation between the degree of difficulty and SPW.  A subsequent comparison with the existing state-of-the-art BERT-based WSD model, Sense LSTM, is conducted, with our model exhibiting superior performance across 9 out of 10 datasets.  A subsequent evaluation of our model on a large-scale open-source WSD dataset, with over 26,000 instances, spanning 20 domains and comprising 10,000 unique words, demonstrates average F1-score performance of 57.3% when employing BERT and 62.9% when combining BERT with hypernyms' definitions. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at 6.16 TeV and 8.16 TeV. Top quark pairs were identified in the lepton+jets final state with transverse momentum above 400 GeV, and rapidity up to 3.5. The measurement lies within the range of previous predictions made based on proton-proton and heavy-ion lead data. A comprehensive study of factors affecting the production cross-section is ongoing. The observed top quark pair production cross-section at 6.16 TeV is 45 nanobarns and at 8.16 TeV is 34 nanobarns, with an uncertainty of 9%. The findings are significant as they open the possibility for studying the production mechanisms of heavy quarks in proton-nucleus scattering and provide a crucial benchmark for future measurements in heavy-ion lead collisions. The research was based on data collected in 2016 by the CMS experiment as part of the LHC's proton-lead run. The measured cross-section exceeds the expected result from combining proton-proton and heavy-ion lead data with an average of 3.5 times uncertainty. The researchers noted the importance of verifying the reliability of their measurement due to the limited nature of their data set. The observed cross-section aligns with heavy-ion lead predictions made under the assumption that the initial overlap zone behaves like a quark-gluon plasma. The findings also support predictions based on calculations that take into account the characteristics of the proton-lead collision's initial state. The researchers identified the dominant formation subprocesses of proton-lead top quark pairs based on their calculations, with the majority arising from gold-sized quark-gluon plasma-like regions within the collision's initial overlap zone. The research concluded that further studies are necessary to gain a deeper understanding of heavy quark pair production in proton-nucleus collisions. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. The findings have far-reaching implications, suggesting that the neutron delta 2s orbital is active in all low-spin Ni isotopes, and that the monopole tensor interaction is crucial for shaping their low-spin structures. The study's results also predict more excited states in 64Ni, and similar patterns of shape coexistence in other Ni isotopes. The extensive data from four experiments used in the research has been compiled into a single figure for easy reference. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. The associated cost is mainly reflected in the prolonged training time required. Furthermore, our findings are supported by the inclusion of an empirical comparison with the conventional k-fold CV approach. The findings are also applicable to other machine learning tasks beyond NLP. The term "effort" used in the theorem presented can be interpreted as the product of J and K, providing a practical guideline for striking a balance between this effort and the desired model performance. The proposed j-k fold CV method is demonstrated to be both simple and effective, with the associated algorithm freely accessible online. The study highlights the widespread occurrence of performance estimation's instability in deep learning models, a phenomenon often overlooked in the presence of continuously improving hardware. In the course of the investigation, the term "easy" was used to describe tasks that are unaffected by the proposed method, however the precise criteria used to classify a task as "easy" or not remains undefined in the study. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening to rigidity transition. Crucially, this approach has been shown to accurately model viscosity across multiple dimensions, providing a tangible pathway to incorporating theories of the shear jamming transition into their analysis.
