Modern Web search engines like Google use personalisation to tailor search engine ranking rankings for individual users based on their search history, location, and account settings. Although beneficial for daily needs, this phenomenon has limitations when it comes to discovering novel information. In this study, we investigated the impact of Web search personalisation on the diversity of search results and consequently, the likelihood of discovering new information. Furthermore, we explored how different search behaviours are affected by Web search personalisation and, in extension, how they correlate with the degree of diversification needed to uncover novel information. Our findings suggest that Web search personalisation effectively suppresses the retrieval of relevant, previously unvisited web content by limiting the scope of searched information to approximately 5-10% of all available online content. In essence, it constrains users to visit the same familiar websites repeatedly. This exclusivity exacerbates the problem of missing out on novel information and presents a challenge for everyday discovery. The underexplored nature of Web search personalisation's effect on everyday discovery has significant implications for our understanding of this phenomenon and calls for the development of search engines that balance personalisation with diversity and novelty. In this study, we suggest a simple yet effective method of enhancing the diversity of search engines in order to facilitate everyday discovery. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. However, more research is needed to fully explain the complexities observed. The drag experienced by the cylinder moved parallel to its long axis was found to be similar to the drag experienced by a flat plate moved in the same way, with the drag in this situation increasing more quickly with speed than algebraically. The drag experienced by the cylinder moved perpendicular to its long axis was found to be similar to the drag experienced by a long cylinder moved in the same way, with the drag in this situation also increasing more quickly with speed than algebraically. The drag experienced by the cylinder moved through the granular bed was found to be influenced by the viscosity of the grain bed, with this viscosity varying greatly depending on the speed the cylinder was moved at. The results of this research could be applied to better understanding the movement of long solids through sedimentary environments, and the insights gained could also be useful for more broadly understanding the flow of sediment around irregular objects. The research was conducted in a way that allows the findings to be compared with the results of previous research conducted in water. The parameters used in this research are listed in the appendix. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Our findings were further validated by comparing our results with experimental data, showcasing the multiphase transport model's capability in replicating triangular flow's magnitude and dependence on transverse momentum. Lastly, we extracted information on the quark-gluon plasma medium by calculating triangular and elliptical flow within the model, and our findings agree with NSTAR and PHENIX's measured values.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. These advancements build on earlier research and have been obtained through comprehensive examination of 20.3 ${\rm fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at 8.16 TeV. The ATLAS collaboration has established strict lower bounds on rare decay rates and refined measurements of CP-violating parameters. Specifically, this has resulted in a significantly tighter upper limit on the $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ branching fraction and more precise determinations of the $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$ effective lifetimes and CP asymmetry, respectively. These findings have important implications for the study of lepton-flavour and CP symmetries within the Standard Model and potential deviations from it.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. The scheme's stability, preservation properties, and practical applicability are validated through numerical experiments conducted on a range of PDEs, including Schrödinger and Allen--Cahn PDEs. The proposed method is also found to compare favourably with other preservation-based time-stepping methods. The study identifies suitable tolerance-based preservation validity regimes for the iteration, and provides a framework for which conditions must be met in order to enforce specific property preservation criteria. The proposed iteration scheme is an accessible and efficient tool for a broad category of applications, given its minimal assumptions and flexibility. The code for the proposed scheme is openly available. The iteration scheme is known as the Preservation-CG iteration scheme. The study also explores and explains the close relationship between the proposed scheme and the Newton iteration. The Preservation-CG scheme can be implemented using the AZTEC library within the PETSc suite, and includes a range of features such as the option to employ a preconditioned version of the scheme, as well as the choice of different polynomial interpolation methods. The proposed scheme is capable of maintaining preservation of specific properties of the solution with even a loose tolerance, and is efficient enough to be applicable to large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. The study further examines and validates the preservation properties of the scheme for a range of different test problems, and includes examples of both one-dimensional and two-dimensional problems, as well as problems with different types of boundary conditions. The proposed scheme is also capable of maintaining preservation of specific properties of the solution even in the presence of noise, and is capable of approximating solutions to PDEs with irregular solutions. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. This benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. Our proposed method, Adversarial Metric Learning for Self-Supervised Scene Flow, leverages a metric structure that distinguishes genuine points from an overabundance of misleading neighbor points, thereby enhancing the efficiency of point selection for optimal feature extraction. This results in our efficiency-based method ranking first in the real-world evaluation. When combined with shallow feature extractors, our proposed method achieves superior performance across all datasets in the benchmark. Moreover, by selectively choosing points based on motion trajectory, our method sets a precedence for downstream task improvement, as evidenced by activity classification results. The proposed method, AMLSFF, alongside the newly introduced scene flow benchmark, has been made publicly accessible.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies within containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly detailed filter policies for modern, complex applications with many processes and threads. Developed using standard Java programming language elements, the Timeloops framework comprises three key components: (1) a low-overhead, binary-only dynamic agent capable of being integrated into the target program, (2) a learning-based component in charge of determining permissible system calls based on the program's behavior, and (3) a command-line interface for program developers. In order to effectively learn behavior for a program, Timeloops employs a combination of Q-learning and a more advanced deep learning-based approach known as DQN. The developed Timeloops framework was put through a series of testing scenarios, including containerized versions of popular web applications, Java-based microservices, and a Java-based implementation of the Memcached memory object cache. The resulting data evidence confirms that Timeloops is not merely a practical solution but also significantly more effective than alternative static analysis-based techniques. The developed Timeloops framework source code has been made freely accessible to the public via GitHub open-source repository management tool. The underlying research work was funded by the National Science Foundation. The conducted testing proved Timeloops to be compatible with the AWS Elastic Beanstalk cloud platform. The research findings associated with Timeloops also led to the creation of a new concept known as Policy-free Containerized Microservices Cloud Orchestration. This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. A concise proof of the desired observability inequality is provided, followed by an exploration of the implications it holds for the controllability of the original system. Furthermore, we conclude by highlighting the potential applications of this controllability result to real-world problems. Lastly, a numerical solution to the inverse problem of determining a minimal set of controllable domains is also presented.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. Furthermore, we examine the possibility of 
using a phase plate to circumvent the limitations of an almost-corrected TEM. 
Results indicate that a phase plate with a charge distribution featuring a 
parabolic pattern, in conjunction with a delta function, can reduce the beam 
divergence to near 1 Angstrom. However, achieving this level of precision proves 
challenging due to the constraint of constant electrostatic surface potential. 
Alternately, we propose a delta function phase plate design capable of minimizing 
the beam divergence to approximately 1.5 Angstrom. Lastly, we analyze the charge 
distribution of a phase plate designed to mitigate the beam divergence to 1.5 Angstrom
 with no delta function, thereby allowing for electrostatic surface potential 
variance. Nonetheless, overcoming the 1 Angstrom barrier through phase plate design 
appears elusive. Nevertheless, we acknowledge the possibility of designing a 
phase plate to attain 0.9 Angstrom resolution. Moreover, we propose an array of 
phase plates each optimized for specific resolutions ranging from 0.6 to 1.4 Angstrom.

Moreover, we establish the asymptotic behavior of solutions in this model and its relation to the solitary wave state, examining under what conditions these solutions remain invariant over time. Finally, we outline the key results from our research on the coupled system's (family of solitary waves, anharmonic oscillator) orbital stability, establishing that this stability is equivalent to the solitary wave family being nondegenerate and stable in a broader sense. Additionally, we offer a concise version of this equivalent condition. The research paper in question builds upon prior knowledge of the Klein-Gordon equation and anharmonic oscillator, incorporating results on their respective solitary wave states and their corresponding stability criteria. The nonlinearity in the anharmonic oscillator is assumed to be even, with a specific symmetry property, and the coupled system's initial data are required to possess this same symmetry property. The research paper in question is organized as follows: section 2 delves into the coupled system's formulation, section 3 outlines the spectral stability of the solitary wave state, section 4 examines the asymptotic behavior of solutions in this model, and section 5 conducts an in-depth analysis of the coupled system's (family of solitary waves, anharmonic oscillator) orbital stability. The research paper also includes two appendices with supplementary information on the linearized equation's spectrum and the anharmonic oscillator's long-time behavior. The findings from this research paper are applicable to a broad class of anharmonic oscillator models. This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We demonstrate how contextualized language models
incorrectly assign different levels of change to words with stable meanings
that have undergone no semantic evolution, thus contaminating the
quantitative data. We further illustrate that the contextualized language model
preference for more recent meanings also mistakenly prefers later occurrences
of words with constant meanings, influencing the qualitative results.
Consequently, our analysis highlights the importance of employing suitable
methodological controls when utilizing contextualized language models to
investigate the nuances of diachronic semantic change. We also explore the
effectiveness of introducing a control for stylistic changes using backtranslation
and find that it significantly reduces the contextualized language model's
sensitivity to recent or less frequent word occurrences.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) occurs. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed light microscopy to examine IKNM in developing zebrafish retina. By applying a quantitative approach that analyzes the movement of individual cell nuclei, we determine the average speed of nuclei migration and discover distinct speed patterns for different retinal layers. Notably, we find the fastest migration speeds in the most primitive layers. Additionally, we identify a slower, more random movement of nuclei within each layer, which we term "interlayer mixing." By distinguishing between these two processes, we determine the respective contributions of directional migration and interlayer mixing to the retinal layer formation. In particular, we find that the combination of these processes generates a parabolic pattern of layer formation. Furthermore, we discover that the random movement of nuclei is the primary factor contributing to "layer skipping," a phenomenon observed in some instances where nuclei bypass one or more layers without settling within them. In summary, our findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding the mechanisms underlying IKNM and suggest that the movement of nuclei during IKNM is a diffusive process influenced by the retinal tissue's architecture. This diffusion is further modulated by the random movement of nuclei, which gives rise to layer skipping and interlayer mixing, and in turn, results in the formation of the characteristic parabolic pattern of layers in the developing retina. This pattern is also susceptible to disruption by increased random movement of nuclei, which can lead to "retinal layer chaos" and, as a result, layer skipping and irregular layer formation. This study on zebrafish retina provides the first quantitative analysis of IKNM, and its findings are likely relevant to other developing neuroepithelial tissues. This research also introduces a light microscopy approach that utilizes a high-speed capture rate to accurately track the movement of individual cell nuclei during IKNM. This method, which uses a 4D reconstruction algorithm to analyze the complex movement of nuclei within the retinal tissue, can be applied to the study of IKNM in other developing neuroepithelial tissues. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Moreover, our complex network's compactness enables physical insights, revealing that the optimal transformation is concentrated in the most challenging region of the phase space. By utilizing this neural network, we are able to solve the self-consistent Compton scattering equation in the (t, J) Hubbard model with a severe sign problem for much smaller Nχ compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, this complex network is effective in reducing the effective temperature, thereby improving the accuracy of simulations with a mild sign problem. Our novel architecture is also capable of modeling any smooth function, offering broad applicability to other Monte Carlo methods affected by numerical integration challenges. We have made the code for this complex neural network publicly available.

Moreover, ReCross is capable of tackling multi-task generalization with remarkable success, also surpassing prior record achievements. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Additionally, we establish connections between these boolean complexes and known structures, specifically the poset of regions derived from a hypercube, and the lattice of order-automorphisms of a poset with specific properties. Lastly, we examine the particular case of boolean complexes based on the hypercube of size n, demonstrating that their homotopy type is equivalent to a collection of (n-1)-dimensional spheres with radius 1. Diana Stewart and Matthew Briggs previously reached this same conclusion in 2020 using a distinct approach.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. To prevent the spread of malicious information, our study suggests implementing targeted interventions aimed at reducing anxiety-driven propagation. By analyzing geographic distributions and examining specific rumors, we found that rumors often adopt a polarization pattern, spreading rapidly in some areas while being suppressed in others. This polarization is frequently dictated by local circumstances and may contribute to the formation of anxiety-driven propagation patterns. To prevent the dissemination of rumors, it is essential to address these underlying local factors rather than simply imposing blanket regulations. In conclusion, this study provides a starting point for developing and evaluating machine learning models capable of predicting the evolution of online rumors, offering actionable insights for authorities seeking to control their spread. Ultimately, by understanding the dynamics of rumor propagation and validating the effectiveness of machine learning models, this research paves the way for more targeted and effective strategies to prevent the spread of online misinformation.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we design a straightforward yet effective strategy for discovering optimal loss functions and apply it to a real-world problem, achieving results that surpass state-of-the-art benchmarks. Our findings are accompanied by an open-source code to facilitate further exploration and replication of our results. We also explore the limitations of our approach and identify potential pitfalls for future research to address. Ultimately, our work is intended to encourage a more flexible, data-driven methodology for selecting loss functions and spark a return to the explicit justification for loss function choice that was prevalent in the early days of neural networks.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to the Cauchy stress and heat flux. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables numerical implementation via a computational framework commonly used for similar problems. The proposed model and its underlying numerical methods have been validated through comparative analysis with existing models and numerical solutions. The research also delves into the simulation of a time-dependent strain-induced crystallization problem, demonstrating the proposed model's ability to replicate problem-specific phenomena. The associated numerical solutions and simulation results have been validated through the comparison with experimental data and other numerical solutions. The research has also explored the simulation of a solid-state strain-induced crystallization problem, which exhibited periodic crystallization patterns and related temperature changes. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification.

The findings also illustrate that the ratio of the non-zero reduced density matrix's trace to the trace is an invariant that doesn't change even when the universe's model changes. The term "invariant trace ratio" is proposed to describe this property. The formula for the quantum capacity can be re-expressed as an invariant that is independent of the universe's model and can be referred to as the "cosmological quantum capacity." Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  The comprehensive nature of ATOMIC is further underscored by our discovery that nearly a million rule-based descriptions are required to adequately capture the complexity of everyday reasoning.  We have made ATOMIC available to the public for the purpose of advancing natural language processing through the inclusion of inferential knowledge.  Specifically, we have outlined a series of tasks and models designed to showcase its potential utility.  These experiments were conducted using datasets that we have developed in-house, namely CTR and AI2-ThoughtChamps.  The former comprises text-based descriptions of conditional relationships, whereas the latter is comprised of multiple-choice questions centered on everyday events.  We believe that both of these datasets hold value in their own right and are capable of being employed by other researchers.  In conclusion, the introduction of ATOMIC marks a significant breakthrough in the development of artificial intelligence capable of everyday reasoning, and it is our hope that it will serve as a foundation upon which more sophisticated models of this type are constructed.  We have open-sourced the code and dataset at https://github.com/uwdata/semtasks.  Additionally, we have created a user-friendly website dedicated to ATOMIC at https://atomic.data.uw.edu/.  We intend to regularly update both the dataset and the results of subsequent experiments conducted using ATOMIC in the future.  This will be accomplished through the maintenance of the aforementioned website.  We have proposed nine categories of conditional relationships as the building blocks of everyday reasoning, and we encourage other researchers to employ them in their own work.  We believe that the effectiveness of models trained on ATOMIC is directly tied to the inclusion of all nine categories, and we have provided supporting data to substantiate this claim.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in finance that requires the maximization of returns while minimizing risk, modeled as an objective function to be minimized. This task is computationally complex and is often resolved using approximate methods. The widely employed mean-variance portfolio optimization follows this pattern and is generally approximated by covariance matrices due to the sheer amount of data in typical financial scenarios. The speed of these calculations can be significantly enhanced using the HHL quantum algorithm. Despite this, the HHL algorithm is hindered by its limited practicality for a variety of reasons, including the difficulty of obtaining precise inverse Fourier transforms and the constraints of the limited number of qubits available in NISQ devices. This paper addresses these challenges by dividing the optimization process into two parts: one classical and efficient part and one that involves the HHL algorithm with a restricted search space. By implementing this strategy on the Wigner distribution portfolio optimization method, we are able to demonstrate a tangible way to reduce the complexity of the quantum portion while minimizing the search space, thus making it compatible with the capabilities of the IBM Quantum Hardware. Moreover, this approach yields a superior investment portfolio when compared to the classical benchmark methods. This research was conducted using the 53-qubit IBM Quantum Hardware and the Google Tensor Processing Units. This is not the first demonstration of HHL on real hardware, but rather it represents an actual finance-based application of the kind of hybrid quantum-classical approach that can be scaled to larger quantum devices. This paper also includes an open-source quantum portfolio optimization platform written in Q# and capable of running on the IBM Quantum Hardware following the NISQ-HHL algorithm. This platform is adaptable to a wide range of financial portfolio optimization tasks and can be run on the Microsoft Azure Quantum Notebook platform. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. Moreover, our model excels on the Switchboard benchmark, cutting the word error rate from 28.4% to 12.3%. The model also demonstrates high performance on the Google's Wav2Vec2 Limited Vocabulary Speech Recognition Benchmark. The code for this project has been made publicly accessible on GitHub.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a specific sequence related to uniform parking functions, a well-ordering known as $PF_1$. We establish that the first elements of this sequence, when considered modulo their smallest non-trivial interval, exhibit almost sure convergence as they approach infinity. Furthermore, this convergence is deterministic and can be explicitly defined. Additionally, we determine the probability distribution that governs the first elements of $PF_1$ within their smallest non-trivial interval. This distributional result has implications for the convergence of the first elements of $PF_1$ when not taken modulo that interval. Lastly, we discuss a related sequence based on the standard ordering of natural numbers and contrast its behavior with that of $PF_1$. This comparison highlights a significant difference in their respective distributional properties. Both sequences share a common initial segment, which we term the base of a partial order. The structure of this base is crucial in distinguishing between different behaviors of ordered sets. Lastly, we outline some open problems related to this research.

The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but also exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The study of a 2 nm thick nanowire showing significantly different behavior with a much smaller critical voltage threshold is also presented. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. Existing 'well mixed' models, while computationally efficient, require key airflow parameters as inputs in order to accurately model the behavior of bus-based transmission dynamics. In the absence of such data, these models may overestimate the degree of bus-based transmission in scenarios similar to the urban bus example examined here. With a better understanding of the limitations of these models, along with the essential airflow characteristics they omit, future public health guidelines are likely to be more precise and effective in preventing the spread of airborne diseases in similar environments.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers in proximity to heavy metals like Bi or Pt. In this study, we examine a Bi/Co multilayer to gain a deeper understanding of how interface scattering influences SOPE and SOC. By constructing a 3-layer structure consisting of Co in the middle and Bi on the outside, we were able to measure the SOPE and calculate the SOC strength in the outer Co layers. Our calculations indicate that the SOC strength in the outer Co layers matches the value in the 3-layer structure, which has no interface scattering. Conversely, in a 5-layer structure with the same construction, interface scattering resulted in a 50% reduction in SOC strength in the outer Co layers. This 5-layer structure also exhibited a different magnetic dead layer thickness compared to the 3-layer structure, further highlighting the complexity of this system. This research highlights the difficulty of controlling the SOC strength in heavy metal ferromagnetic layer structures due to the overwhelming impact of interface scattering caused by the heavy metal's strong scattering nature. As a result, it may be challenging to achieve the desired SOPE and SOC in these structures, which could have implications for their use in controlling spin-orbit coupling and related phenomena in the adjacent layers. This finding also emphasizes the significance of using the 3-layer structure as a reference in future research on heavy metal ferromagnetic layer structures. In addition, this discovery suggests that heavy metal ferromagnetic layer structures are inherently different from the 3-layer structure and may be more analogous to the 5-layer structure, with the possibility of both 3- and 5-layer structures existing in the same sample, with the 3-layer structures located at the interface and the 5-layer structures in the bulk. This could result in the heavy metal ferromagnetic layer structures exhibiting both interface and bulk SOPE and SOC. This possibility is supported by the presence of both interface and bulk Anomalous Hall Effects in the Bi/Co multilayer sample used in this study. This could have far-reaching implications for heavy metal ferromagnetic layer structures and related physics, with the need for further research to fully understand this complex physics. This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. The analysis indicates that the generalised potential model fractal behaviour yields measurable energy shifts and does not significantly affect the bound state eigenvalues, but may influence the discrete spectrum in the potential well. The paper also highlights the importance of choosing appropriate fractional differential definitions, particularly in physical applications, where mathematical approaches must correspond with measurable, real-world phenomena. The analysis further illustrates that the chosen definition of fractional derivative, in this case the Jumarie type, leads to solutions with physical implications, whereas alternative definitions, such as the Caputo type, result in solutions with singular terms that cannot be physically interpreted. The paper also highlights the scope for further research into the Riemann-Liouville type of fractional derivative, which may lead to additional, previously unconsidered physical solutions. The analysis of a harmonic oscillator with a fractional mass parameter $\alpha$ is also presented, with the corresponding energy eigenvalue calculations for this model given. The paper also discusses the relationship between the ground state energy eigenvalue calculations for this model and the parameter $\alpha$, with the added mass fraction $\alpha$ causing a shift in the ground state energy eigenvalue calculations. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the optimal weight range that satisfies a network's desired level of input sensitivity. This approach enables us to leverage existing optimization frameworks for training neural networks. Our experiments reveal that imposing a moderate level of input sensitivity does not significantly impair a neural network's efficacy, and in some cases, it even results in performance improvements. Moreover, we found that this approach is particularly effective in mitigating the adverse effects of overfitting on small image datasets. Interestingly, our findings also demonstrate that imposing strict input sensitivity on deeper neural networks is challenging and may result in them failing to converge, a problem we encountered in our research. This failure to converge is attributed to the difficulty of optimizing the weight range within the imposed constraints as neural networks of this depth tend to require more precise control over their weights. This research is distinct from existing work on training neural networks to be Lipschitz continuous using spectral normalization, which was demonstrated to result in improved performance on large image classification datasets. This is shown to be a misinterpretation of the training network's desire for greater input sensitivity due to the similarity between spectral normalization and enforcing a network's input sensitivity. Rather, as hypothesized in this research, it is actually a result of the similarity between spectral normalization and imposing a regularizing L2 penalty on the network's weights, which in turn reduces overfitting. This is corroborobated by the findings of this research, which show that imposing a regularizing L2 penalty on the network's weights results in similar performance improvements on the TNIST dataset used in the MNIST experiment. This research is also distinct from existing work on training neural networks to be bi-Lipschitz continuous, which was demonstrated to result in improved performance on small image classification datasets when using an alternative optimization approach. This research further explores the efficacy of enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity by training it on bi-Lipschitz continuous data, which was found to be ineffective. This research also examines the relationship between imposing a network's input sensitivity and dropout, which was found to be unrelated. This research also examines the efficacy of imposing a neural network's input sensitivity using an alternative optimization approach, which was found to result in performance improvements on the TNIST dataset used in the MNIST experiment when reducing the learning rate. This research further explores the efficacy of imposing a neural network's input sensitivity on the CIFAR-10

To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. To facilitate such searches, we provide a program that generates precise corrections to Drell-Yan ditau production, along with pseudorapidity distributions of ditau systems. This code is an essential input for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of PET-MRI acquisition configurations and scan protocols. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model, demonstrating improved image quality and reduced segmentation error when processing data outside of its distribution. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study finds that these computer systems perform poorly on tasks that are relevant to CT, such as determining the central statement in a text. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful features from a set of signal distance metrics that can be used to train a regression model to predict the actual distance between these data sets. The proposed solution, tested using random forest and gradient boosting regression models, yielded a mean absolute error of 16.5 centimeters. Furthermore, the model exhibited strong generalization capabilities, extending to untested outdoor spaces, and the feature extraction process identified the indoor space dimension as a critical factor in estimating geospatial distances. The proposed model demonstrates a 25 percent reduction in estimation error compared to the widely accepted Euclidean method. The novel approach developed in this research is suitable for use in a wide range of indoor environments with minimal need for calibration, making it an ideal choice for deploying WiFi-based distance estimation algorithms in real-world applications. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, the research highlights potential safety margins that can be set based on specific machine designs, eliminating the need for a general beam current constraint. The findings presented can be applied to various energy recovery linacs, including those used in proton therapy, ion acceleration, and advanced free electron lasers. The research underlying this paper was conducted at the Center for Advanced Accelerate Engineering at the University of Texas at Austin. The associated data can be found at [1, 2]. The term energy recovery linac refers to a type of particle accelerator that, as its name suggests, recovers energy from spent particle beams rather than discarding them. The term is often abbreviated as ERL. The beam breakup instability in question specifically affects linear accelerators, particularly those with long sections of the type found in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. The phenomenon occurs when an accelerated beam is diverted and sent into another part of the machine where it interacts with an RF system, causing unwanted oscillations that can destroy the machine or reduce its effectiveness. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have been well-established for flat and spherical surfaces, but lack a comprehensive explanation for polymer brushes attached to curved, complex surfaces, such as those found in rolled-up nanotubes and parabolic microchannels. This study resolves this uncertainty by demonstrating that a highly elongated brush attached to an arbitrary curved surface will always exclude a specific inner circular region, regardless of the surface's complexity. By assuming a highly stretched brush state, we used numerical methods to solve the self-consistent field equations and obtained the shape of the excluded zone for various curved surfaces, including those with positive and negative curvature. This general understanding of surface brush geometry provides valuable insights for channel and nanotube design, where optimal filling, adhesion, and fluid flow can be achieved through the controlled elongation of grafted polymer brushes. This research also offers a practical solution for recovering rolled-up nanotubes by identifying the ideal brush lengths to ensure tube unrolling. Furthermore, our findings related to the filled brush geometry in parabolic microchannels may contribute to the understanding of blood flow dynamics in narrow blood vessels. The principles outlined in this study can be applied to a broad range of brush geometries, extending beyond curved surfaces to those with periodic undulations and random topographies. The concept of an end exclusion zone can be visually represented as a 3D'molecular finger print' that reflects the unique brush geometry, offering a straightforward method for inferring the shape of the excluded zone from the brush's molecular structure. The general framework of this research, based on the fundamental brush geometry equations, enables researchers to derive the excluded zone geometry from any arbitrary brush configuration. The precise calculation of the free energy of the brush also remains accessible within this framework. The research presented in this study has been conducted in close collaboration with experimental colleagues, involving the comparison of calculated excluded zone geometries with the actual shapes observed under an electron microscope. The open and versatile nature of this model allows for its direct application to a wide range of real-world scenarios, as well as its use as a prototyping platform for the development of new brush geometries in various technological contexts. The general principles outlined in this study can be extended to a broad range of problems related to the curved and stretched brush configurations, offering a groundbreaking achievement in the field of polymer brush research. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. It turns out this property is equivalent to graphs being k-connected. Also we find the metric dimension of trees of a specific depth and show that within these trees, the largest identifying sets are those including the leaves at a particular distance from the trunk. Furthermore, we establish that determining the minimum identifying set of a graph is NP-hard and review some notable examples of beta_k for commonly occurring graph types. Lastly, we discuss the relationship of this property to another, known property of graph resilience. Lastly, we propose several open questions about this graph property.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models also successfully highlighted variable sources, such as those known to change over the week-long period, with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling helping to quantify the sources' fluctuation patterns. By prioritizing variable sources, the model was able to highlight sources with significant weekly modulation, and by prioritizing the image sharpness, it highlighted sources with daily or longer-term variability. The team found that the most variable sources were concentrated towards the galactic center but noted that the distribution of sources with daily or longer-term variability remained uncertain. The improved image quality and source extraction enabled the detection of weaker sources with daily or longer-term variability, and the research highlights opportunities for combining machine learning image processing with traditional methods to enhance current surveys for variable sources. The associated code and data are readily available, and the research paves the way for applying similar techniques to other gamma-ray telescopes. The team estimates that a year's worth of data could be processed on hundreds of GPUs within a week, and they suggest combining the sharpened image with the point source catalog through likelihood profiles to enhance the accuracy of source spectra measurements. The novel approach has the potential to directly benefit next-generation telescopes with wide-field capabilities that will be able to observe large areas of the sky with high sensitivity for short-term periods. The research is also applicable to other instruments with wide-field capabilities in different energy bands. The team found that the dictionary learning model replicated the spatial distribution of the 68Si target in the galactic center and suggested searching for target sources within 5 degrees of the center in the 68Si energy range. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems. The serial mechanism involves a linear ordering of participants, where each is given a turn to make a choice, with their selection being based on previous choices. When a student-project allocation problem is considered, with projects benefiting from being paired with specific students, we establish that finding an optimal serial dictatorship is equivalent to solving a specific flow augmentation problem in network flow theory. Furthermore, this optimal ordering can be efficiently determined in polynomial time. In contrast to this controlled environment, we also prove the general case of determining the best serial dictatorship for any optimization problem to be NP--hard. Additionally, the paper includes an examination of its affine-equivalent formulations and related precision on optimal orderings. With its accessible and intuitive framework, the serial dictatorship mechanism now joins other notable methods like greedy algorithms and the knapsack method as a problem-solving tool. With its straightforward and intuitive nature, this mechanism is poised to find applications in a broad spectrum of optimization domains. The precise parameters of its affine equivalence may also provide insights into the underlying structure of specific problems. The paper's findings are further illustrated with an example from the U.S. Congress's committee assignment issue. The research for this paper involves an extension and the generalization of an earlier results for a specific student-project allocation problem presented in "Serial Dictatorship for Project-Student Allocation" by the same authors. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, with both methods enabling the detection
of binary asteroids by identifying offset peaks within the collapsed profile or 
distinct elliptical PSF orientations synchronous with the asteroid's movement. 
By applying these methods to approximately 1.5 million images and combining the
results with existing binary records, we identified 13 new probable binary 
asteroids within the main belt, with diameters ranging from 10 to 50 kilometers 
in diameter. Notably, our analysis also revealed a one-to-five binary ratio in 
relation to single counterparts, together with preferential detection of large 
binary asteroids towards the sun, near the L5 Jupiter asteroid trojan point, 
and within the Kirkwood gap between Jupiter and Saturn. Further in-depth 
investigations into these findings and additional large binary asteroids are 
essential to refine our point spread function analysis techniques, and to 
better understand the sun-directed transport of binary asteroids, and the 
originating mechanisms driving their formation. Based on this research, we propose
a simple method for creating point spread function analysis datasets from similar
deep wide-field surveys featuring slowly moving small objects. The associated
data, detection criteria, and point spread function analysis code are available
online at https://github.com/astrobanner/PANSTARRS-Binary-Asteroid-Candidate-List.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. The trefoil knot folding landscape is further expanded upon this finding, suggesting that the crossover from a deep to a shallow knot topology might arise from a critical temperature that is linked to protein stability. Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. Additionally, under the assumption that the irrationality criterion is universally met, the same conclusion is reached for all one-point symplectic blowups of $T^4$. A significant aspect of our proof involves establishing that the action of the mapping class group on the first relative cohomology group is uncountably vast when it exhibits a specific infinite divisibility property, which in turn leads to the desired irrationality and consequently the desired infinite cardinality. The unanticipated achievement of our investigation is the exact determination of this cohomology group as a Lie group algebra specifically isomorphic to $so(3)$, which we believe to be a novel and interesting discovery. The research that preceded this project by Alperin, Caglar, Draghici, Eskin, McMullen, Mirzakhani, and Mohammadi is invaluable to our work.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The counterfactual data produced is versatile, enabling efficient incorporation of new perturbation types without additional supervision. The code for this framework is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/nytng/disco. Moreover, a pre-trained model is available on Hugging Face Model Hub at https://huggingface.co/nytng/Disco-CAUT-LM.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The technique has practical value in real-world applications.  All the code used in this research is available for public use.  A novel challenging dataset known as face-sentences was also introduced, ready for multi-label segmentation task challenges.  This new technique has potential applications in multi-condition GANs.  The technique can be used in conjunction with the existing methods, notably the single positive loss, to enhance performance. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would require a different mechanism.  The model's success in accounting for the energy spectrum in the galaxy Mrk 421, a jet-powered blazar, highlights the overlap between these two phenomena.  The areas of these galaxies that are not covered by jets still need explanation, suggesting that this model is part of a broader phenomenon affecting black holes in the present day universe.  The prediction that the gamma-rays in the galaxy IC 310, a quiescent jet, should be powered by a star forming-driven supermassive black hole rather than radio or optical means could be tested through observations.  The possible link between the absence of gamma-rays in faint, low-mass black holes and the lack of gamma-rays in the galaxy Sgr A* and the universe's earliest generations of stars also require further investigation. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose. However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices. To address this challenge, we evaluated the effectiveness of several features and machine learning classifiers in cardiac sound analysis with noisy recordings. Specifically, we examined the impact of different training sets and recording conditions and tested two low-frequency recording protocols. Furthermore, we investigated the role of preprocessing techniques such as filtering and dynamic time warping in heart sound classification. Our experiments on the PhysioNet detection of acute aortic dissection dataset revealed that frequency-weighted filtering enhanced the results when using a large training set to make predictions about low-frequency recordings. Additionally, we found that a specific recording protocol associated with SphygmoCor devices had a 100% classification accuracy with simple techniques like filtering and dynamic time warping. Our research highlights the importance of considering recording protocols and conditions when developing algorithms for cardiac sound analysis and suggests that such protocols could be convenient alternatives to deep learning models like convolutional neural networks. Consequently, our findings have implications for the design of deep learning models and stress the need to provide detailed information about recording protocols in future cardiac sound classification challenges. Lastly, we propose a new approach called the convolutional neural network with protocol information, which integrates recording protocols directly into deep learning models to enhance their performance.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of this type of data. However, training models on user-owned data is challenging due to constraints on uploading large amounts of data and the need for sensitive medical data to remain private. Additionally, individual data sets lack diversity. A federated learning approach overcomes these limitations by training models on user data while keeping it on local devices. However, it struggles to perform well on a single dataset. This paper proposes FedHealth, the first federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare. FedHealth combines a vast amount of background data available in the public domain with limited amounts of user data to improve model performance. It utilizes a significant amount of public domain data only to train a initial model and sets up a compact dataset for efficient data storage on individual devices. FedHealth reduces storage requirements on devices by half while maintaining comparable model performance. It also leverages user data to calculate personalized loss weights, enhances model generalizability, and introduces a drift detection mechanism to ensure smooth model updates in presence of changing user data. This paper explores various transfer learning approaches within FedHealth, compares their efficacy, and provides practical guidelines for implementing the framework. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FedHealth. It achieves comparable performance to non-federated models while reducing storage requirements on devices by up to 70% and ensuring secure and private healthcare services. This is particularly useful for low-function devices like smart wristbands. FedHealth also provides valuable code and models for real-world healthcare applications. It has been successfully employed in various projects such as developing a platform for renting out unused computing power in vehicles and an intelligent bike sharing system. This framework has the broad potential for applications in various healthcare and mobility projects. It has been made available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Shuai-Luo/FedHealth.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of stable states arising from a class of autonomous systems subject to these abrupt cost transitions. Finally, our research provides a starting point for exploring similar problems involving abrupt changes in system dynamics rather than cost structures.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, including the radius r itself.
In this research, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance criterion known as the Hamming distance and aim to

This report provides an overview of key mathematical models used during the ongoing pandemic to understand and combat the spread of the COVID-19 virus. Starting with a background on the epidemiological parameters that define disease transmission, we explain the most prevalent model types - including the SEIR model - and offer critical assessments of their strengths and limitations. Specifically, we examine nonlinear regression-based models, network-based models, individual-based models, and models that account for the psychological impacts of lockdowns. While these models have demonstrated practical value in this pandemic, we also discuss the challenges they pose and the opportunities they present for the field of infectious disease modeling. As the pandemic continues to evolve, we emphasize the need for models that incorporate real-world data and provide timely insights for public health policymakers. This report is intended for readers with a general interest in mathematics and medicine, with the ultimate goal of promoting greater collaboration between mathematicians, healthcare professionals, and policymakers working together to address the ongoing and future public health challenges posed by the COVID-19 virus. With this in mind, we conclude by outlining potential research directions for the field of infectious disease modeling. This report was developed as part of the activities of the Australian Mathematical Society's Special Interest Group for Mathematical Biology.
