Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more quiescent. Since the behavior of the bulge in these galaxies aligns with Hubble types, such as giant spirals lacking bulges and thus still forming stars at high masses, it follows that the M*-SFR relation turns over due to bulge growth, particularly in giant spiral galaxies, by limiting star formation in the central regions. Alternatively, other factors such as the influence of environment could also be responsible for the turn over. Systematic errors in the study may stem from using a single color to determine SFR and using a specific redshift range. Nonetheless, the findings suggest the role of bulges in governing the behavior of the M*-SFR relation in the high mass range is significant, but not exclusive, and more research is necessary to confirm these results.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, differing interpretations of image features complicate the process. Machine learning models, in particular decision tree-based features, can extract meaningful patterns from radiologist annotations by design. Yet, whether they prioritize clinically significant features indicative of severe symptoms over less important image characteristics requires further examination. In this study, we employed a decision tree-based model to identify key X-ray features associated with severe COVID-19 outcomes in ICU patients following initial analysis by radiologists using the CHEERS scoring system. By prioritizing the most critical image characteristics, we found that certain features are redundant and less predictive of severe symptoms. The model's performance was also notable, with an AUC-ROC of 0.85 in predicting ICU admission. The findings provide a foundation for creating a more efficient, clinically relevant scoring system to streamline the imaging process and allocate resources more efficiently. Additionally, by prioritizing the most predictive image features, this study takes an important step towards creating more effective AI models capable of accurately predicting severe COVID-19 outcomes based on X-ray images. The model's simplicity, with a limited number of features, makes it more interpretable and less prone to overfitting, further contributing to its clinical relevance. The study's results and insights are valuable to the medical community, radiologists, and AI developers alike, with the potential to improve clinical decision-making, streamline imaging protocols, and develop more effective AI models for predicting severe COVID-19 outcomes. The model is available for use in the Middle Eastern country of study and has the potential for broader application worldwide. The study's findings also highlight the importance of incorporating clinical expertise in the development of AI models, with the potential benefits of such collaboration on improving model performance, as well as providing education and training for radiologists on the optimal features to annotate in X-ray images of COVID-19 patients. The study further proposes the development of a more advanced model, incorporating additional features extracted from lung density analysis, to predict the progression of COVID-19 outcomes in ICU patients. The model's performance in predicting ICU admission in this study is comparable to other published works, with the study's novel contribution in hand-tracking, lung-density analysis, and mass-spec features integration yet to be evaluated by other researchers. The model's limitations provide potential areas for future research, with the potential for machine learning-based approaches

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. In response, we developed a method known as Easy-VRD, which tackles VRD as a dual object detection task. By simplifying the task in this manner, we significantly reduced the true positive rate but, in turn, greatly decreased the false positive rate. To address the issue of low true positive rates, we introduced a hard example re-weighting technique called Inscribed VRD. By re-weighting the model's importance for difficult relationship predictions, we increased the true positive rate while maintaining the low false positive rate achieved with Easy-VRD. Our method demonstrated superior performance on the COCO-VRD dataset. When applied to the VRD task on the VOC dataset, Easy-VRD attained a 25% absolute increase in relationship recall with only a 3% absolute rise in the number of incorrect relationships. On the iNaturalist dataset, Easy-VRD showed a 15% absolute improvement in species recognition accuracy with a 10% absolute decrease in false positives. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang34/Easy-VRD.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing "inside-out" quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, may have triggered their quiescence through bar formation and subsequent bulge construction. If confirmed, this could indicate that the balance between star formation and quenching is affected by gas accretion and tidal disruption, and that the relationship between disk asymmetry, quenching, and bulge construction may have remained relatively unchanged since $\rm z\approx3$. If further supported by additional data, this hypothesis can be put to the test, potentially with the added benefit of better understanding the evolution of the universe's mass composition. Indeed, if quiescent galaxy populations at $\rm z\approx 3$ were similarly biased towards lopsided systems, then the mass density of biased, quiescent, lopsided bulge-forming galaxies would be minimal, implying that the universe's mass composition is primarily composed of ordinary matter rather than dark matter. If proven incorrect, this could alternatively suggest that galaxy interactions and mergers that form bars and bulges are significantly more prevalent at higher redshifts. Consequently, this discovery encourages further observation and analysis, particularly with the upcoming Generation VI telescopes that will be capable of observing similar galaxy formations at even higher redshifts.

Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. As this event occurred at a lower altitude than previous discoveries, it highlights the limited range of which high-energy solar neutrons can travel through the atmosphere. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and ruled out any possible uncertainties in the core radius calculation. Additionally, we examined possible variations in the rotation rate over time and found no evidence of change within the measurement accuracy. Lastly, we explored possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum transport deep within its interior. Although our research cannot exclude other factors that could shape its internal rotation, we found that planet engulfment or a recently discovered deepening angular momentum transport mechanism in low-mass stars offered the most plausible explanations for its rotation pattern. Given the limited knowledge about this predicted angular momentum transport, we propose calling it "Differential Internal Angular Momentum Decoupling" (DIAMD), which provides a rotation profile that is linear with a negative slope in a way that aligns with DIAMD profiles and offers a distinguishing feature to better understand this predicted phenomenon. Key findings from this research are subject to verification, and we encourage further investigation into this and other rotating giant stars to validate our results and gain a deeper understanding of this predicted DIAMD phenomenon. If confirmed, this predicted phenomenon could shape the rotation patterns of low-mass stars that have expanded into giants. Furthermore, it provides a distinguishing feature for low-mass stars with prolonged planetary interactions and offers a characteristic rotation pattern that can be used to identify them. This phenomenon may also offer insights into the mechanisms that shape the migration paths of such circumbinary companions and influence the subsequent evolution of their host stars. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the constantly evolving nature of false news necessitates a memory-based approach to store the knowledge gained from previous events. In this research, we propose a novel framework called MMFEND, utilizing meta neural process networks for fake news detection that addresses these challenges. The proposed network comprises three key components: a hypernetwork that generates an initial parameter to predict the common content, a neural process that learns the individual content, and a read-out module that produces the final output. The MMFEND network is trained using a meta neural process objective function, ensuring that it can effectively learn from a limited amount of data from any event. The proposed framework has several advantages over the existing methods, including the ability to handle events with limited data and detect false information on previously unseen events. Moreover, MMFEND can handle events with different labels, reducing the constraint of having labeled data for each event. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction is a distinctive feature of silicon and may have implications for silicon-based quantum technology.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles. Despite the simplicity of these underlying laws, real-world applications often reveal complex, seemingly random behaviors. In this work, we develop a new approach that involves treating each component's behavior as a distinct, individually explainable entity, which can be understood through Graph Neural Networks. By individually deciphering the inner workings of each component, we can combine their distinct functions to reconstruct the full complex system and its dynamics. This approach enables us to break down complex phenomena into their fundamental components and gain a deeper understanding of the underlying structures and dynamics governing them. In a real-world analysis of the global electricity grid, our method reveals key insights into the spatial distribution of power generation and consumption, the electrical connections between different regions, and the temporal dynamics driving the system's instability. Our research introduces a novel, universally applicable method for analyzing complex systems and their dynamics, coupled with a practical application that sheds light on the intricate relationships and temporal patterns within the global electricity grid. This has implications for how we interpret and model real-world phenomena and provides a platform for further research in areas like power grid stability and optimization. We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Additionally, our methodological approach yields an alternative proof of a known formula related to the Euler characteristic and related counts, specifically $\chi_{2^n}(q)$. Moreover, our approach can be applied to enumerate the coefficients of a particular power series, specifically the dual of the mod $2$ Milnor-Moore invariant polynomial associated with the symmetric group $S_n$, thereby confirming a conjecture proposed by M. Welker.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in this task, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with different characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the treatment evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure known as the rooted tree directory, devised to streamline rooted rule checks and review the compiler's time complexity. Moreover, the compiler now generates forward references to improve memory efficiency. A customized tool has also been developed to visualize the executable code and derived abstract syntax trees, facilitating a deeper understanding of the executed program and providing a graphical representation of the program structure. This tool and the improved GP 2 compiler, along with example programs and the compiler source code, are available for download at www.isa-acc.org/software/.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. Our comprehensive framework's application in low-dimensional data embedding results in outstanding performance, surpassing rival methods in both unsupervised and supervised settings as evidenced by the obtained results.

However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In order to improve the speech enhancement experience, the DPCRN model was developed to simultaneously work on both short-term and long-term signal patterns. Combining a convolutional neural network's ability to analyze local signal characteristics with a recurrent neural network's capability to model sequential data patterns, the DPCRN model consists of two distinct paths processing the left and right channel inputs independently. Each path includes a convolutional encoder, a classification-based auto-encoder, and a convolutional decoder to reconstruct the clean signal. Objective evaluation results reveal the DPCRN model surpasses state-of-the-art models, and the source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrjy/DPCRN. Moreover, a lightweight version of the DPCRN model was created, which outperforms existing models in the evaluation. The model's efficiency makes it suitable for real-world applications involving limited computational power. The evaluation of the DPCRN model on the REVERB19 dataset also demonstrated its superiority over existing models. The model can be trained using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 for 60 epochs, with a batch size of 128, and provides good results at a relatively low computational cost. The model's performance in the noisy test set, which simulates real-world conditions by introducing 5ms of random delay, showed only a 0.04 reduction in the objective evaluation score. The DPCRN model's simplicity and high performance make it an appealing choice for real-world speech enhancement applications. The model's lightweight version can be trained on a single GPU within 2 days, with a computational requirement of 16000 GPU minutes. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that have long been deemed unnecessary, and alleviate issues like convective instability seen in some current schemes. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring descending and ascending fluids, both dynamic and coupled through the Euler equations, with the aim of replicating atmospheric Rayleigh-Benard convection when a heated surface warms the bottom of a closed chamber from below. By comparing the model's output with the classical two-dimensional, open Rayleigh-Benard problem, the paper highlights the applicability of the multi-fluid framework in capturing the core features of this problem, albeit with the presence of spurious ascents near the sides of the chamber presented in the experimental setup used to mimic real-world conditions. The model's performance serves as a stepping stone for further refinement, with the aim of resolving the boundary layer directly. The paper also explores the implications of the model's side wall ascent and the presence of the boundary layer on the efficacy of the scheme, with the purpose of identifying potential paths for improving the multi-fluid algorithms used in the model. The results obtained from the model, along with the underlying physics and the mathematics of the multi-fluid equations, are the foundation for the development of the next generation of mass-flux free convection schemes. The paper at large presents the multi-fluid solution to the problem of closed Rayleigh-Benard convection in a way that is accessible to the broader atmospheric science community, with the aim of fostering interdisciplinary collaboration between atmospheric scientists and the researchers who develop these schemes. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Moreover, this finding extends to other JC-like systems, suggesting it may have broader implications. Lastly, we propose a measure that determines the degree to which the unconnected system's state becomes genuinely multipartite entangled.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Lastly, we propose that the shadow radius can be used as a thermodynamic variable in its own right, with attributes similar to those of the horizon radius. However, it behaves uniquely due to its dependence on the shadow radius's exterior geometry. We also examine the relationship between the shadow radius and the thermal behavior at the black hole's surface, which is characterized by a temperature gap when transitioning from the small to big black hole phase. This gap persists even as the shadow radius and the horizon radius become identical, an occurrence that happens when the nonlinear YM charge parameter value equals 1, which is also the value at which the shadow radius most closely approximates the horizon radius. This unique behavior of the shadow radius allows it to exhibit thermal hysteresis even when the radii values are identical, providing additional insight into the complex thermal behavior of black holes. We propose that the shadow radius can be used as a "shadow thermometer" to monitor the thermal behavior of black holes. This thermometer is unique because it is based on geometry rather than temperature, and it detects thermal hysteresis even when the temperature gap has closed. This is the first known instance of thermal hysteresis being detected in black holes, and it occurs when the parameter that defines the nonlinear electrodynamics charge also equals 1. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Our findings show that changes in entanglement and synchronization manifest as distinct patterns in the optical tomogram and provide a basis for detecting these phenomena without the need for full state reconstruction. We achieve this goal by introducing a dimension that represents the phase space and using a machine learning-based approach to train an analyzer capable of extracting the relevant dimension from the optical tomogram, thus facilitating the efficient detection of these phenomena. 360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating valuable information from video
subtitles, this model's precision in predicting user views is significantly
improved. Experimental results confirm that the inclusion of subtitles in the
prediction model leads to a notable 23% improvement in accuracy when compared
to the existing method. Moreover, the model's efficiency is also enhanced with
a decrease of approximately 24% in its computational complexity. The proposed
approach can be applied to a broad spectrum of 360-degree streaming videos,
particularly those featuring guided tours. The model's performance can be
further improved by utilizing more advanced subtitle-based features, as well as
other available streaming video data. The source code for the proposed model
is available at https://github.com/zhengyang106/VPEDOT.

By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. Additionally, we offer a brief glimpse into the potential expansion of our method to include surfaces defined by hyperbolic equations. In the course of our investigation, we also encounter a surface defined by a hyperbolic equation that resists linearization, presenting an intriguing problem for further resolution. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. The code is available at https://github.com/ghulghul/CoImitationLearning.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement. This generalization, which we've termed as the 'action similarity layer hypothesis', along with reducing action spaces, constitutes our proposed framework for a setup resembling real-world NMT scenarios. This framework's efficacy is validated across multiple benchmarks including the widely used WMT English to German dataset. With only two expensive reinforcement learning steps, our proposed framework is able to achieve the same level of performance as a critically acclaimed NMT model, whereas typically 5 to 7 steps are required. Our proposed framework also extends seamlessly to multi-grammar translation, as our research demonstrates. This framework is available online at github.com/PranavT1591/RL-NMT-LargeActionSpaces.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces that shift the system's energy 
levels can lead to unusual directions of current flow.
Moreover, our theory highlights unique over-shooting points where the system's 
non-equilibrium steady state current flows in an opposite direction compared 
to the driving force's speed.
Our analysis also reveals distinct non-equilibrium steady state and phase 
behavior when the system's energy levels are shifted at different frequencies 
in a periodic manner. Our results further demonstrate that discrete time-driven 
dynamics systems exhibit distinctive features that are undetectable in their 
continuous time-driven counterparts. Our research was conducted using a highly 
coherent driving force, allowing for precise control over the system's energy 
levels and enabling the development of practical quantum amplifiers that can 
detect extremely weak signals. Our findings are applicable to a broad spectrum of 
quantum systems, encompassing a wide range of driven systems, from those with 
many degrees of freedom to individual quantum systems like the qubit in question.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. We open-source our approach and the pseudocode for the protocols in question. In replica set deployments, we found that the protocol actually implements a variant of multi-version concurrency control rather than a variant of snapshot isolation. This distinction has significant implications for the consistency guarantees provided by transactions in these deployments. Our findings highlight the importance of scrutinizing the source code of database management systems, rather than relying solely on official documentation, when conducting a deep analysis of their transactional protocols. This approach to verifying the consistency of database transaction protocols can be applied to other similar systems. We also discuss the implications of our discovery for the practice of documenting database transaction protocols. The pseudocode and verification proofs for the MongoDB transaction protocols are available online at https://github.com/ Formal-Verification-of-MongoDB-Tx-Protocols/. The approach we took to verify the protocols is described in detail in the README file for that repository. The README file is also the sole output of our approach as evidenced by the Docket file. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our study on data from four different closeness measurements to see how the solar wind energy flux changes with distance from the sun. Combining this with data from the Effective Temperature of the sun and the speed of the solar wind, we were able to map the solar wind energy flux across the inner heliosphere, and compared it with computer simulations of the solar wind. These comparisons helped us better understand the workings of the inner heliosphere, and specifically the region between 1 and 5 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and revealed how the solar wind energy flux varies with distance from the sun and how it was affected by different approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe. Additionally, we found the angle of the solar wind speed and solar wind energy flux to the sun's rotation axis to be nearly the same, which is likely the result of the conservation of angular momentum within the solar wind. The solar wind energy flux decreases by half as we move from 0.3 to 5 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and the speed of the solar wind also slows down by half within the same distance range. The solar wind speed and solar wind energy flux both become more focused on the equatorial regions of the sun at distances closer to the sun, which may be caused by solar magnetic field changes near the sun's equator. The data from the solar wind plasma instrument on board the Parker Solar Probe also provided the most detailed measurements yet of the solar wind energy flux within the inner heliosphere, and these findings have important implications for the study of similar solar wind environments around other stars. The research from this study has been used to improve the accuracy of computer simulations of the solar wind and the magnetic field near the inner edge of our solar system, which in turn has helped in the analysis of close approaches to the sun by other spacecraft. The study from this research has also been used to better understand the workings of the solar wind and the magnetic field within the inner heliosphere, which has important implications for the safety of future close approaches to the sun. The findings from this research have been used to improve the training of computer algorithms that simulate the solar wind

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package includes features to simulate a wide range of phenomena, from pure noise to complex signals, with various spectral and spatial patterns, as well as various levels of missing or faulty data. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Moreover, the MD-CSDNetwork exhibits superior performance when dealing with fewer training examples, indicating better robustness and generalizability. The code for this research has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghr95/MD-CSDNetwork.

This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. Moreover, the quantum group U_q(g) is topologically generated by the cluster X, thereby obtaining a topological basis \bar{χ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Finally, we establish that the quantum group U_q(g) is topologically isomorphic to the quotient of the cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘) by the ideal I_θ, which has a basis consisting of quasipolynomials with real coefficients. This research was motivated by the conjecture proposed by Kostov, along with an alternative proof by EiHiro. Additionally, it yields an explicit formula for the quantum dimension, which is defined as the structure coefficient of the unit 1 within the basis \bar{Θ}. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions within these scams, it has been extremely difficult to gather comprehensive data on a large-scale pyramid scheme. Our research fills this gap by examining Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, and we have gathered detailed information on its design, operation, and financial impact. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible transaction data, our analysis utilizes cryptographic pseudonyms (address aliases) to uncover the underlying peer-to-peer sales networks for each version of the scheme. Our findings reveal that the financial returns for a significant number of participants were actually negative, with the majority falling into the lowest ranking categories of the scheme. By comparing two versions of the scheme, we observed that increasing investment rewards led to an explosion in new recruitments but also caused a significant slowdown in existing participant upgrades, ultimately harming the majority of participants even more. Our analysis also identified distinct peer-to-peer sales networks for each version of the scheme, further underscoring the scammer's minimal financial gains. Lastly, our data reveals the scheme's ability to attract and deceive a constantly flowing stream of new participants, with the majority being drawn in within a week of the scheme's launch. The transparency of blockchain technology and the public nature of the smart contract permits us to demystify the inner workings of a pyramid scheme, and the data on Forsage is substantial, with over 100,000 participants and over $13 million in invested funds. The research presented in this paper is relevant to a broader audience interested in cryptocurrency, blockchain technology, and financial scams. The methodology used here can also be applied to analyzing other similar scams built into smart contracts. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of undercomplete coding in autoencoders, positing that a well-formed sentence can be accurately represented by a sparse set of words. This notion serves as the foundation for SparseGAN, the first GAN model to generate concise sentences with relevant content. By incorporating a carefully designed embedding layer and a parameterless discriminator, SparseGAN delivers superior performance, surpassing leading neural text generation models, including PPL-GAN and TextGAN, according to evaluation metrics including BLEU, METEOR, and CIDER. Moreover, our model exhibits reduced training costs and generates more compact sentences with higher effectiveness. Software required to run this model can be obtained at https://github.com/nyuVLabs/SparseGAN. Evaluate results are available at arxiv.org/abs/2011.01675.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal and also account for space-use behavior.  However, these models require no prior understanding of target species' space-use habits.  Our research integrated resource selection functions into the Bayesian spatial capture-recapture model to gain a deeper understanding of how animals select spaces that are easy to inhabit and to infer population density.  By doing so, we enhanced the model to also estimate parameters for resource selection functions.  This model can be useful for conducting simultaneous studies of low-density populations that inhabit large areas and has the added benefit of providing more accurate population density estimates.  We also developed a new method for visually analyzing model-estimated probability density surfaces and compared it to existing methods.  Furthermore, this model can be applied to multi-species capture data to estimate the density of individual species.  We tested and validated our model using simulated and real capture-recapture data.  Real data consisted of acoustic surveys for bats, presenting a challenging case study with dense vegetation that makes it difficult to define study areas and with low detection probabilities that change over time, and with space-use behavior that differs among species.  Our model successfully applied to this complex scenario and provided accurate estimates with low bias.  Our research provides R code for capturing and analyzing data.  Our model has several advantages over existing methods and can be a valuable tool for conducting further research on complex wildlife populations.  Such research involves investigating space-use behavior in large areas with diverse habitats, analyzing multi-species capture data, and conducting simultaneous studies of low-density populations that inhabit large areas.  In these scenarios, with diverse and complex habitats, it is difficult to define areas and to gain accurate population density estimates with low bias.  Our model can also reduce the time and financial costs associated with capture surveys by conducting acoustic surveys with shorter duration.  This is achievable with the added benefit of gaining a deeper understanding of space-use behavior with low bias.  Our research provides a novel approach for estimating the cost of capture surveys with shorter duration.  This, in turn, can further reduce the time and financial costs associated with capture surveys. We examine the concept of "galactic intelligence," defined as the ratio of a galaxy's optical brightness to its physical size squared. By doing so, we calculate "intelligence" values for a subset of spiral and irregular galaxies using historical photometric data and modern stellar mass estimates. Our results show that "intelligence" varies significantly across the galaxies studied and does not differ on average between spiral and irregular galaxies of a similar type. However, when accounting for elements like carbon, oxygen, and silicon, we find a positive correlation between their abundance and low-frequency "intelligence." If we interpret "intelligence" as a form of Bayesian intelligence, this relationship makes intuitive sense, as it would indicate galaxies rich in these elements are more likely to contain long-lived low-metallicity generations of stars rather than massive short-lived high-metallicity ones. On the other hand, the negative "intelligence" of many galaxies could suggest they contain significant amounts of gas that fail to participate in star formation. The possibility that "intelligence" might simply reflect characteristics like central mass concentration or the presence of massive black holes is also considered. Ultimately, "galactic intelligence" is found to be a complex and multifaceted property that resists a single explanation and may need to be redefined in a more nuanced form. The methods developed here can be applied to larger galaxy datasets and with more precise mass estimates and modern photometry. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The developed framework has implications for various applications related to biology, ecology, and conservation, along with potential uses in the fields of computer vision and robotics. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders, composed of two types of disorders with different signs, on a one-dimensional tight-binding chain. Our research reveals that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged tail distribution and winding number's overlap, which can be visually demonstrated with numerical simulations. Furthermore, our findings show that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, also reflecting the clean topological phase's characteristics. Additionally, we discover localized states at the edges of one-dimensional chains with the Sheng-Yin-Wu topological Anderson insulating phase, consistent with the clean dimer model's behavior. This result can be understood by analyzing the localized wave function and the Chern number's behavior along the disorder parameter's variation. Notably, binary disorders' effect on the topological Anderson insulating phase appears robust when correlated disorders are replaced with uncorrelated ones. This research was published in "Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter".

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, and provides an explicit lower bound on this ratio for any $K$, establishing it as proportional to the minimum of the $K^{th}$ largest or the second largest integer value in the set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$, also known as the $K^{th}$ order statistic. This bound can be visualized as a "gap" within the distribution of extremal power control values, and is further illustrated through a theoretical example. This research was initially presented at the IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory in 2019 under the title "The Extremal GDoF Gain of Optimal versus Binary Power Control in $K$ User Interference Networks Is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$".

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for faster computation, multiple-step integration methods are commonly employed, however, these methods can produce inaccurate results when used to simulate particle collisions, especially in high-speed flows. In contrast, our multiple-step integration method simulates collisions through the application of impulse forces resulting from real physical collisions, and it is compatible with a wide range of flow solvers, including those using the lattice Boltzmann method. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height, and reduced errors in force and trajectory compared to a pure feedback control system. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the efficiency and stability of the system were demonstrated by achieving the same height with 30% less peak power and reducing ground reaction force discrepancies by 75%. Ultimately, this research showed that effective force and position control is possible even on uncertain, deformable terrain. The DEM simulation model and the corresponding control system can be adapted to other legged robots navigating similar terrains. The current model and control system also have implications for the design of robot feet and their interaction with granular materials. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating hadronic and quark phases using the Polyakov-loop non-local chiral mean-field model, we obtained the density dependence of sound velocity and the quark phase's possible realization.  Furthermore, we established a critical compactness boundary for stars experiencing a deconfinement transition, with approximately 1.4 solar mass quark stars as the maximum possible star type.  This research was presented at the 19th European School of Astrophysics and the 13th Pan-European Research Institute on "Physics of Relativistic Ion Interactions and Relativistic Astrophysics".  Our findings relate to compact stars' density ranges, with quark stars exhibiting sound velocity maximally 0.4 lower in density ranges 2-10 times nuclear saturation density, and possibly realizable in the laboratory with heavy ion collisions.  This work highlights the potential for sound velocity and density relationships to distinguish quark and hadronic phases in compact stars.  As such, this research supports utilizing compact stars as laboratory equivalents for matter at extreme densities, with implications for ongoing and future heavy ion collision and multi-band X-ray observations. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also offers Heisenberg limited estimation precision. Additionally, we find that both small amounts of photon loss and imperfect displacement measurement do minimal harm to Heisenberg limited sensitivity. Sifting through the various states for those with the smallest quantum footprint, we pinpoint those with the lowest number of contributing Fock states, offering a means to scale Heisenberg limited estimation to a broader range of scenarios. Lastly, we examine preparation probability barriers that stem from the compass state's unique structure and advise on strategies for overcoming them.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered a 17% decrease in recidivism among offenders who received mental health treatment.  This reduction in recidivism held true across various demographic groups, including both violent and non-violent offenders, and was found to occur within a one-year time frame following the completion of the original sentence.  However, it's worth noting that the available data did not account for the content of the treatment or the offender's mental health status prior to treatment.  The study identified costs associated with court-ordered mental health treatment but found that it was less expensive than imprisoning these offenders.  In contrast to paying for treatment, imprisoning these offenders for one year was found to be approximately 5 times more costly than paying for court-ordered treatment.  The estimated annual savings for North Carolina's justice system following the implementation of this policy was approximately $18 million.  The findings suggest that court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation reduces the likelihood of an offender returning to the justice system and is a more cost-effective approach than imprisonment.  The research also highlights the justice system's potential to function as a platform for delivering mental health services to individuals in need.  However, to enhance the effectiveness of this approach, the study recommends gathering more detailed information on court cases and offenders receiving treatment. The degree of disorder in a material's crystal structure significantly influences its electronic properties and, as a result, local bonding behavior. To effectively train neural networks to identify the local bonding configurations of atoms within a material's crystal structure, we employ a graph neural network paradigm that assigns unique vector representations to individual atoms based on their local surroundings. This method allows for the direct comparison of vector representations associated with atoms in different materials' crystal structures, facilitating the quantitative assessment of local bonding disorder. We introduce an interpretable metric, the vector distance coefficient (VDC), which calculates the similarity between the vector representations of atoms in two different materials' crystal structures and quantifies the degree of local bonding disorder in a material. By applying this approach to previously well-characterized and unknown materials, we demonstrate the VDC's effectiveness in identifying materials with local bonding disorder and categorizing the degree of disorder in materials with known defect concentrations. Further analysis reveals the VDC's relationship with other disorder metrics and the local electronic and lattice structure in materials with and without local bonding disorder. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. The study also compares the convergence rates of FedBuff with and without bounded gradients in realistic scenarios. Moreover, the study demonstrates that the algorithm delivers satisfactory performance in real-world scenarios across multiple datasets. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our ultimate Czech model achieved an impressive 8% WER decrease when compared to the original system. Our method's success was also reflected in its ability to adapt to Prague English data, resulting in a notable 4% WER reduction. We believe our findings have significant implications for establishing strong Czech ASR systems with limited data, as well as implementing practical, cost-effective solutions for other less familiar languages. We have open-sourced our code and trained models on GitHub.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating synthetic data to train models. However, relying on synthetic data may lead to inaccuracies and necessitates significant amounts of information for effective learning. In contrast, few-shot domain adaptation allows for the exploitation of existing expertise. We propose a novel approach that employs meta-learning for adaptation, leveraging knowledge from a source domain to enhance performance in a target domain with limited data. The underlying architecture consists of a weighted sum of source and target transformations, with weights determined by the task. We further introduce a style-invariant representation to mitigate lexical differences and enhance the attention mechanism's sensitivity to structural errors. The proposed method was evaluated on the NME dataset and achieved superior results for both zero-shot and few-shot learning compared to existing GEC methods. Furthermore, an analysis of the proposed method's components through ablation studies demonstrated their individual contributions to performance improvement. With the integration of a pre-trained language model as the encoder, the integrated model showed a notable increase in performance in both zero-shot and few-shot learning settings. Additionally, a discussion on the relationship between meta-learning and style-invariant representations through the lens of a latent variable is presented. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and no fair algorithm can guarantee an approximate pure Nash equilibrium for all possible instances, especially considering general valuation functions, has been well-examined. However, when we enter the realm of combinatorial domains, which include allocations of graphs, paths, and trees, the problem of finding a pure Nash equilibrium becomes significantly more complicated. In fact, it's known that, for a wide range of combinatorial domains, there's no fair algorithm that can efficiently produce an approximate pure Nash equilibrium for valuations within a particular range. In our research, we delved into the specific case of allocating paths to agents and discovered a fair and efficient algorithm that could generate a pure Nash equilibrium for a broad class of valuation functions. Moreover, this approach allows us to determine the optimal fairness parameter when dealing with valuations within a particular range. The beneficial consequences of this discovery include the attainment of both efficient and fair outcomes in tasks like spectrum allocation and selling routes to self-interested agents. The pure Nash property of our algorithmic approach based on path-completeness also facilitates the establishment of approximately fair outcomes in various combinatorial domains. The research also includes an intriguing result where, for a particular valuation function, the reduction of the fairness parameter to its optimal value enables the emergence of a situation with no regret for the agents in the combinatorial domain of paths. The efficiency and the property of no regret for a particular valuation function can be sustained for a duration of $\tilde O(n^5)$ time steps, whereas the transitions between these situations take $\tilde O(n^3)$ time steps. The discovery of a situation with no regret for a particular valuation function in the combinatorial domain of trees in $\tilde O(n^9)$ time steps in our additional results also warrants note. The approach we took to achieve these outcomes involves utilizing the method of allocative and computational pure Nash equilibria based on path-completeness. The insight gained from this discovery, specifically the property of no regret for a particular valuation function in the combinatorial domain of paths, can be sustained for a duration of $\tilde O(n^5)$ time steps, and the transitions between these situations take $\tilde O(n^3)$ time steps. The discovery of a situation with no regret for a particular valuation function in the combinatorial domain of trees in $\tilde O(n^9)$ time steps in our additional results also warrants note

limits due to variations in the source's emission behavior. By analyzing the

affected its integral to the accretion rate. Combining our measurements with
similar data from other sources, we found that the spread in accretion rates is
