Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulghul21/SIT.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Furthermore, this model exhibited a broader range for capturing correspondences. To apply this network in 3D, we introduced a new post-processing technique, patch-based 3D voting, to generate accurate and natural-looking 3D results. Additionally, we explored a parameter that affects the quality of 3D results and provided a guideline for its selection. The training dataset consisted of 1000 pairs of randomly divided brain images, utilizing a Dice score of 0.87 for 2D and 0.83 for 3D models, respectively. Lastly, we conducted an experiment with megavoltage images from a linear accelerator, yielding satisfactory outcomes. The code is available at: https://github.com/ghasemianm/MV-Image-Registration.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of the EPR paper in 1935, Einstein had already raised these concerns. The phrase'spooky action at a distance' was, in fact, coined by Einstein himself. Throughout this paper, we will explore the idea that the phenomenon Einstein found so unsettling can, in fact, be viewed as a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, demonstrating the incredible potential of the non-local, the'spooky,' phenomenon resulting from the entanglement of two particles. In particular, we will concentrate on the genuinely non-local effect produced by the entanglement of single particles, known as steering. The paper is organized as follows: in section 2, we will examine the EPR experiment and the associated concerns about the completeness of quantum mechanics; in section 3, we will delve into the history of the infamous Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of the 1935 paper; in section 4, we will explore the phenomenon of steering and its distinction from entanglement; in section 5, we will discuss the genuinely non-local effect produced by the entanglement of single particles; in section 6, we will examine the relationship between the EPR experiment, the associated concerns about the completeness of quantum mechanics, and the phenomenon of steering; in section 7, we will concentrate on the fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics demonstrated by the'spooky' phenomenon resulting from the entanglement of single particles; in section 8, we will explore the potential applications of the phenomenon of steering; in section 9, we will examine the connection between the phrase'spooky action at a distance,' the associated phenomenon, and the related historical context; and in section 10, we will conclude the paper. The purpose of this paper is to highlight the incredible potential of the non-local, the'spooky,' phenomenon resulting from the entanglement of two particles, in particular the genuinely non-local effect produced by the entanglement of single particles, known as steering. The paper is intended for experts in the field of quantum mechanics with an interest in the historical development of the subject and the potential applications of the non-local, the'spooky,' phenomenon.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and has the potential to operate seamlessly within IoVs frameworks. With the emergence of trusted Federated Learning models utilizing blockchain technology as a platform, research has explored its potential in securely and privately sharing IoVs data with various entities. This paper conducts an in-depth review of current research on IoVs data shared via a blockchain-enabled Federated Learning platform, and goes on to outline potential applications and offer a roadmap for future research in this field. Moreover, this study provides a comprehensive knowledge base that stakeholders, developers, and academics working on IoVs and related technologies can draw from.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Numerical evaluation demonstrates the scheme's efficacy across different GMM configurations and mobile speeds. Moreover, by analyzing coding gain and robustness, it becomes apparent that prioritizing coding gain or robustness in GMM training is crucial for performance improvement. Furthermore, codebook size's impact on system performance is also examined, revealing that a smaller codebook size can provide comparable performance to larger sizes, with reduced data transmission, making it an attractive solution for bandwidth-constrained scenarios. The proposed method's applicability extends to time division duplex (TDD) systems, with some codebook size-specific adjustments, and evaluation results for this case are included. The proposed scheme's efficacy across different FDD and TDD scenarios provides a solid foundation for adapting codebook feedback schemes to real-world scenarios. The code for this research can be found at \url{https://github.com/ghasemzade/GMM-Codebook-FDD}. The proposed method has the potential to be further developed into a more advanced machine learning-based codebook feedback scheme, with possibilities for utilizing different models, such as k-means or deep neural networks, to construct codebooks. The scheme's robustness to various parameters makes it an ideal starting point for such extensions. In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to solve this complex problem by breaking it down into simpler sub-problems that can be solved at the encoder, relay, and at the noisey channel end. We also test these theories with realistic simulations. The outcomes indicate that in the single user, single relay scenario, the amplitude of sub-carriers should decrease linearly from highest to lowest, whereas in the multi-user, multi-relay case, the optimal distribution is more complex and varies greatly depending on the number of users and available frequencies. The simulation results also demonstrate that a decrease in signal-to-noise ratio leads to a frequency distribution shift towards a more even distribution. The findings of this research are relevant to wireless communication technologies that employ dual hop OFDM technology. The investigation demonstrates that there are optimal ways to manage frequencies in a secure wireless communication system that uses dual hop OFDM technology, and it also highlights the positive impact of reducing signal-to-noise ratio on even frequency distribution. The study further emphasizes the benefits of using a noise-robust encoder. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. Moreover, by incorporating sophisticated multi-threading capabilities, TextWorldExpress enables seamless testing across multiple machines, further expanding the testing space available to developers.
Our findings demonstrate that current virtual agents, despite performing well in isolated tasks, struggle significantly when confronted with the complex challenges found in text-based games. Our analysis of treatment plans for existing weaknesses in virtual agents includes refining their ability to follow instructions, improving their problem-solving capabilities, and enhancing their ability to apply real-world knowledge. Our hope is to see the development of more sophisticated virtual agents capable of withstanding the rigorous testing provided by text-based games. Our research and associated findings are made publicly available through open-source coding. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity while minimizing data loss. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that fully leverages the hierarchical nature of the tensor decomposition. The results demonstrate substantial improvements in both the efficiency and effectiveness of the FDHT-LSTM model in video recognition. When compared to conventional LSTM networks, FDHT-LSTM exhibits a notable 87% reduction in model size, a 78% decrease in memory usage, and a 71% decrease in computation requirements. Furthermore, when tested on a customized hardware platform, FDHT-LSTM showed a 4.7 times improvement in frame rate in video recognition tasks. The proposed design also offers great potential for extending its applications to other tasks beyond video recognition. The designed hardware platform as well as the FDHT-LSTM algorithm have been made publicly available on open-source platforms. The integrated algorithm and hardware platform presented in this research set a new standard for the design of high-performance, energy-efficient deep learning models, particularly LSTMs, and provides a customizable solution for various other sequence analysis tasks. We develop a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our method being compatible with nonconforming hybrid finite elements, allowing for precise modeling of blocking fractures without the need for their geometric details. This approach also guarantees satisfaction of continuity requirements across the surfaces of conductive fractures without the need for mesh alignment. This marks the first time a mixed method is employed to model blocking fractures using the Dirac-$\delta$ function approach without mesh alignment, offering significant practical advantages. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the inclusion of numerical examples.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis and provide a critical examination of the Bayes factor estimation process. We discuss the importance of pre-posterior checks on model estimates, the potential risks of overfitting, and the need to assess Bayes factor sensitivity to prior specifications. We also explore the use of Bayes factors to evaluate theories in the context of frequentist power calculations. To facilitate the evaluation of psychological research using Bayes factors, we introduce the R package "RLoCo" which provides a framework for conducting Bayes factor estimation, identifying the optimal sequence of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples, and evaluating the adequacy of model fit. We illustrate the application of RLoCo in the cognitive science context by conducting a simulation study and analyzing actual cognitive science data. We conclude by discussing the limitations of Bayes factor analysis and the potential risks of overreliance on Bayes factor estimation tools. We also outline the RLoCo package development plans and invite users to contribute to the package development process. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To facilitate these results, we introduce a geometric notion called geodesic convexity and show its equivalence to the traditional concept of convexity in the ambient Euclidean space. Finally, we offer a discussion on issues related to optimality and the need for further improvements in the Riemannian quotient geometry. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing word clusters in each language. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/MCSE.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that minimize latency but are less effective in handling large amounts of inertial measurements, resulting in subpar accuracy. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently processing vast amounts of inertial data while focusing on crucial elements, and seamlessly integrating this model with a lightweight image feature extraction network to estimate pose from both the camera and inertial sensors' data. The proposed system was tested on a moving robot equipped with a camera and inertial measurement unit (IMU), and the results show it outperforms the state-of-the-art VIO models, including the ones using recurrent models, in terms of accuracy. Moreover, by minimizing the number of required inertial measurements, it also demonstrates the model's potential to be used with IMUs of a lower specification, making it suitable for more compact setups. The code for this project is available at this link: https://github.com/yuejiaqi1995/EMA-VIO.

Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. The approach is found to be robust with respect to the level of data smoothness required and provides accurate solutions even when the domain's geometry is complex. The examination includes a comparison with the iterative and direct least-squares approaches. The development of the method is further illustrated through an examination of the problem's stationary variant. The application of the method is also demonstrated in a problem of reconstructing an inclusion inside a pipe using boundary measurements on the outer perimeter. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Moreover, FedSA has the adaptability to handle diverse, complex relationships between tasks and data sources. The code for FedSA is available at this link: https://github.com/ghru/FedSA.

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Notably, our findings also apply to families of $A_4$ quartic extensions, filling a prior knowledge gap. This research was motivated by Diophantine equations based on the norm of an $S_4$ quartic field, and a related question about the infinite nature of ranks in $T_4$ quartic extensions.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between distinguishability time and the average system-state's distance from the equilibrium state achieved in a thermalization process. Lastly, we discuss the practical applications of these concepts to two experimental scenarios. The study mentioned above was featured in a related arXiv paper titled: Quantum speed limits and asymmetry flows on the Bloch ball. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$. Special attention will be given to a particular projector $P_{\Delta}$ associated with simplices and a problem will be posed regarding its norm. Additionally, the norm of another projector $P_{\Delta}$ will be determined with the assistance of the Burkurn-Rosenthal inequality. Furthermore, simple recursive formulae will be provided to compute the norm of yet another projector $P_{\Delta}$. Lastly, the paper will conclude by exploring the relationship between the projector $P_{\Delta}$ and the well-known potential theory.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, including those driven by the planet's internal dynamics, solar energy, and external objects. Additionally, we investigate the complex feedback mechanisms that have impacted the atmospheric evolution, with possible implications for the surface temperature and pressure. Current constraints on the timescales of these processes pose challenges for certain theoretical models. A key finding is that many atmospheric processes occur on similar timescales, making it essential to incorporate multiple processes simultaneously in model assessments. Further research is needed to fully understand the atmosphere's evolution, with particular emphasis on refining the timescales associated with key processes and evaluating the effectiveness of various model frameworks. A comprehensive understanding of the atmosphere's evolution is crucial for predicting the planet's future climate and the potential for habitability on other similarly extreme exoplanets. A better grasp of the atmosphere's evolution is also likely to provide valuable insights into the Earth's own atmospheric history. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial power being successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. Additionally, it was observed that a certain configuration of this waveplate could generate a laser pulse that is partially helically polarized, which has a longer duration than the original pulse due to the reduced peak power. This phenomenon has been explained by the way the component interacts with the laser pulse, modifying the plasma density in a way that extends the pulse duration. This indicates that this type of waveplate can also serve as a device for stretching extremely short high-power laser pulses. This concept is straightforward to scale up, making it a versatile tool that can be applied to multiple applications involving high-power laser pulse systems. This includes the enhancement of laser pulse waveforms that are utilized in inertial confinement fusion experiments, as well as in the delivery of high-power laser pulse capabilities to smaller target chambers located at distant points from the main laser system, by stretching the pulse duration to several nanoseconds, which, as shown here, is a capability that this type of waveplate possesses. This can be further optimized to enhance the interaction of laser pulses with matter in various experiments, even extending to the level of modifying the waveform of the laser pulse itself, which has been demonstrated to convert a linearly polarized pulse to a circularly polarized pulse with the same peak power, but with a much shorter duration, which in turn results in a level of plasma interaction that is level of solid density, even at extremely high laser intensities. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. In our experimental evaluation, we found that for code rates less than half, the best rank metric codes alongside the diverse code family exhibited a significant error correction capability, substantially greater than the best Gabidulin codes of the same rate. In contrast, for code rates greater than half, the diverse code family performed significantly better than the rank metric codes. Our results also demonstrate the superiority of the diverse code family in scenarios where the error matrix is not necessarily symmetric. The proposed methods and our findings have implications for the security of certain cryptographic protocols, such as the ring learning with errors key exchange. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a peak absolute magnitude that was 0.3 magnitudes brighter than typical and a longer duration of luminosity decline in its plateau phase than usual. Observations during the plateau phase were characterized by narrow H and He lines with normal line profiles, unlike previous instances. SN~2020jfo also exhibited a prominent asymptotic giant branch (AGB) bump and a long duration of nebular phase, with [Ni II] and [Fe II] lines persisting up to 230 days. Using the semi-empirical relationship between progenitor radius and plateau duration, it's inferred that SN~2020jfo had a large progenitor radius. Estimates of SN~2020jfo's initial mass range from 13 to 17 solar masses, with a likely mass loss range of 8 to 13 solar masses. Analyzing the explosion energy and bolometric radiant energy, it's found that SN~2020jfo fell within the normal range of Type II supernovae. Based on the low iron peak element abundance and the presence of [Ni II] and [Fe II] lines in the nebular spectrum, with a formation time of about 145 days, it's inferred that SN~2020jfo occurred in a massive low-luminosity AGB or an extremely luminous metal-poor super AGB star. With an explosion energy and a bolometric radiant energy that fell within the normal range of Type II supernovae, SN~2020jfo adds to the growing list of supernovae that occurred in massive low-luminosity AGB or super AGB stars. The extensive data for SN~2020jfo also makes it suitable for future training and testing of deep learning models for Type II supernovae. The reduced light curve of SN~2020jfo can be fit with a two-segment exponential model, with a short plateau phase lasting about 14 days and a post-breakout decline rate of 0.016 mag/day^2, while the full light curve, including the initial decline phase, the AGB bump phase, and the nebular phase, can be fit with a piecewise exponential model consisting of five segments. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The MuLE design also allows for the easy incorporation of polarization filters and other accessories, and its optical mirror has a relatively small curvature, making it simpler to manufacture. The proposed optical design can be optimized to detect polarization, and it would be highly suitable for space-based X-ray transient monitoring in the soft X-ray band. The MuLE design can be applied to other types of optics, such as the V-groove optics, and it would significantly reduce the number of image sensors needed even in the hard X-ray band. The MuLE concept can be combined with the focal plane array consisting of pixel arrays, which would further enhance its sensitivity. The MuLE design with 9 segments has an optical efficiency of ~10% or better, and it would be suitable for a wide range of applications, from the soft to the hard X-ray band. To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, the study revealed that the addition of velocity information from the same simulation does not significantly improve the model's performance, despite velocity field influence on halo formation over long periods. By modifying the training data to include the velocity field, the model's accuracy in predicting halo masses was demonstrated to decrease in the low-mass halo regime. Furthermore, by analyzing the parameters of the model, it was found that the average density of the simulation corresponds to the characteristic mass scale, which reflects the power-law relationship between halo mass and the velocity/density ratio. The outcome is consistent with the universal behavior of halos in the $\Lambda$CDM cosmology and the regime in which star-forming galaxies reside. The model's effectiveness was also tested on simulations with different parameters and it showed robust performance. The simple, simulation-derived expression for the halo mass function, which is independent of the specific velocity field and governed by the average density of the universe, is proposed as a valuable alternative to the numerical approach. The findings of this study are relevant to the ongoing and future dark matter halo formation simulations with high resolution, specifically the Distributed Computing Project's LSO and the DOE's NERSC's Arrowhead systems based on IBM BlueGene next-generation architecture. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. Furthermore, our formulation and associated numerical tools are suitable for a broad range of problems involving rotating stars, and our methodology prioritizes simplicity over optimized performance to facilitate easier tool integration and problem expansion. 

Our methodology is paired with the use of the Newton-Raphson method to solve a large set of nonlinear equations, as well as the W4 method developed specifically for this purpose, and is capable of handling a wide range of problems and is easily integrable with external tools. 

We have also generated accurate results for rotating polytropes, Roche lobes, and massive stellar evolution, and our code is notable for lacking any form of Euler equation integral, instead using direct solutions to the Euler and Einstein equations, and our results demonstrate the applicability of this method to solve a range of problems involving rotating and evolving stars.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our findings indicate that models trained with selective labeling methods on smaller datasets composed of simple annotations (such as the CRAFT dataset) can perform equivalently to those trained on larger datasets with more intricate annotations (such as the iTRC dataset). Our approach and accompanying code are available at the website: https://selectivelabeling.github.io/.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of compact binaries, their environments, and the universe as a whole. However, the electromagnetic signatures of most mergers remain unknown, leaving the electrical telescope counterparts for most events undetected. The burden of detection counterpart signals is particularly heavy, with over 900 mergers identified by the end of 2019, surpassing the resources of traditional machine learning methods. To tackle this challenge, we developed an automated system based on deep learning, capable of filtering out likely counterparts for the most promising mergers. This approach takes the full spectral energy distribution of each merger and employs a convolutional neural network in conjunction with a long short-term memory network to identify and label the most relevant electromagnetic features. The system's efficiency enables the automatic generation of customized templates for the detection of electromagnetic radiation from compact binaries across the entire parameter space of merging compact binaries. The developed model yields a year's worth of likely counterparts from the most promising 6% of mergers and prioritizes the most intense electromagnetic signals from the remaining 94%. The predictive power of this model is further substantiated by its successful prediction of previously undetected gamma-ray counterparts. The neural network's insights into its own functioning also provide valuable physical knowledge, with the identification of key features related to jet energy, inclination, and electron density. The model's capabilities make it an ideal starting point for the intensive follow-up observations necessary for multi-messenger astronomy, with the potential to convert the entire population of detected mergers into electromagnetic sources with known properties. The model's accessibility is also demonstrated by its successful deployment on a cloud-based deep learning platform, with the potential for real-time predictions from a wide range of compact binary merger detections. The system's open source code is available at https://github.com/krishnasreni/Compact-Merger-Electromagnetic-Classifier. The model's predictions for the electromagnetic properties of previously undetected gamma-ray counterparts opens up possibilities for observational verification through targeted searches with gamma-ray telescopes, with the potential to convert the model's predictions into detectable sources with known properties. The model's ability to prioritize the most intense electromagnetic signals from the remaining 94% of mergers also suggests that a significant population of compact binaries may emit faint electromagnetic radiation across the entire parameter space

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Additionally, it highlights the significance of considering both physical and social distancing in policy analysis. Lastly, it highlights the difficulty in achieving diverse urban environments in the post-pandemic era with prolonged decreased willingness to explore new places.

Theoretical models suggesting that the most massive stars form quickly are difficult to reconcile with observations showing that massive protostars typically take their own mass in gas to form. One possible explanation is variable accretion driven by gravitational instability in protostellar discs. While disc instability can lead to both accelerated and slowed down accretion, it's unlikely to affect low-mass stars. However, a proc ess called gravitational turbulence could generate turbulence in the disc and influence accretion rates, particularly in more massive discs. Combining this model with observations of molecular outflows and spectral types, we found that the most massive stars formed in the shortest time frames, with the fastest 10% forming in under 20000 years, while the slowest 10% took over 80000 years. This result is consistent with the idea that variable accretion and disc instability influenced the most rapid star formation, although more research is needed to fully understand its effects. Additionally, this model may account for the different frequencies of binary mergers and star formation, with variable accretion potentially leading to the formation of binary stars rather than isolated low-mass stars. If true, this could shift the origins of binary mergers observed through gravitational waves such as GW17gts or GW190425, which are currently thought to arise from isolated binary formations, towards a population influenced by disc instability and variable accretion. Further verification of these findings will require more detailed simulations of protostellar discs and better constraints from observations of protostellar masses. If confirmed, this model also predicts the existence of massive stars formed from the merger of low-mass binary stars, with characteristics that can be identified through spectroscopic analysis of their surrounding discs. If found, this would provide direct evidence for the role of variable accretion and binary mergers in forming massive stars. The expected frequency of these mergers and their resulting stars is difficult to estimate, but it's clear that they would contribute significantly to the population of massive stars formed through this process. The model further suggests that the most massive stars formed through this method would have masses above 50 solar masses, with the exact upper limit difficult to determine but certainly above 100 solar masses. The predicted distribution of binary mergers and their resulting stars also varies by mass, with the most frequent mergers producing the most massive stars, although the exact relationship between them is difficult to define and will require further research to fully understand. The model also predicts the existence of massive stars formed through the direct merger of low-mass binary stars

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to solving the problem, one that arises from the Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian action on the unperturbed Schrödinger equation. This in turn leads to the formation of solitons when the dispersion is sufficiently weak. Our results differ from those obtained through the use of the Korteweg-de Vries equation, specifically with regard to the relationship between the thickness of the soliton and the intensity of the shear flow. Our research on the soliton dynamics demonstrates that the phase shift it causes is directly related to the vorticity of the flow, in addition to showing that the soliton moves at the same speed as the background flow while also experiencing a constant acceleration caused by the vorticity. Our findings on the soliton dynamics are consistent with those obtained through other methods, although they provide a more detailed analysis of the problem. Our approach facilitated a derivation of the Dysthe equation through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian action on the Schrödinger equation, in addition to obtaining an explicit expression for the linearized operator around the soliton solution. This in turn enabled the determination of the soliton's spectrum, specifically revealing that it consists of a continuous part that is identical to the spectrum of the original Dysthe equation, in addition to a discrete part that includes a family of modes directly related to the Vlasenkov equation. Our research on the soliton dynamics also involves a discussion of the effects of the soliton's birth, merging, and decay on the water depth and the underlying flow, in addition to showing that these processes generate a wide range of Vlasenkov and discrete eigenmodes, specifically including their frequencies and the corresponding amplitude relationships between them and the soliton's height. Our findings provide a comprehensive explanation for the numerous harmonic and subharmonic modes that can be observed during these processes. Our research involves a comparison with the results

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here. The abstract differential operator adjoint to the exterior differential, along with the measure it is adjoint to, are then used to prove the Stokes formula for differential forms from one class that form a boundary of forms from another class. This implies that the Stokes formula holds without the requirement for spaces to be compact or the absence of singularities, thereby expanding on earlier results. The paper also clarifies the relationship between the measure defined through differentiation and the measure defined through integration, demonstrating they are equivalent, and shows that the operator adjoint to the exterior differential when acting on differential forms is equal to the surface layer operator when acting on forms that are not differentials, which in turn leads to the Helmholtz decomposition of vector fields without the need for compactness. The paper concludes with the extension of the Stokes formula to forms on spaces with the structure of a product of locally convex spaces. The extension to the product space results in the formula holding for a broader class of measures defined through integration, including those obtained from differentiation measures on the individual product spaces. The paper also includes the expansion of the Stokes formula to the product space, which allows for the derivation of the Holder estimate for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential, along with an expression for this operator and the equivalence of the measures defined through integration and differentiation on the product space, which in turn leads to the Helmholtz decomposition of vector fields on the product space without the requirement of compactness. The paper ends with the mention of the extension of the Stokes formula to the case of forms on Riemannian manifolds with the requirement of compactness of the manifold. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Furthermore, the reduction of sensing diversity to single sonar sensor scenarios demonstrates feasible outdoor application on the layered navigation controller. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter the growing falsehood problem. Our approach employs a dual role for automatic text summarization, utilizing a saliency-based method to highlight crucial sentences and a similarity-based method to integrate important words for our deep learning-based fake news detection framework. The proposed technique demonstrates superior performance in evaluating experiments on two widely used datasets. Moreover, our method showcases the beneficial impact of text summarization in fake news detection by revealing boost in performance with increasing summary lengths. This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on a specific aspect of these systems – their geometric properties – using statistical tools to analyze two different random field models. Unlike traditional random field models, the models studied here do not conform to a specific parametric pattern, making them more challenging to analyze. The study overcomes these challenges by developing a mathematical framework that provides insights into the models' geometric characteristics and reveals an intriguing phenomenon known as the "curvature effect." The "curvature effect" describes how the models' geometric properties change in response to an increase in their underlying random variables. The study goes on to explore the mathematical structures underlying these systems and provides a practical application of the "curvature effect" to the analysis of traffic patterns within the transportation network of Moscow. The research concludes by identifying opportunities for further exploration into the "curvature effect" and its implications for the transportation network of Moscow. The underlying mathematical structures of the random field models used in this study are also introduced in the appendix for the benefit of fellow researchers. When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this point satisfies a weak stationarity condition. As a result, the algorithm produces a minimum of the original smooth convex optimization problem up to a precision controlled by the step size. The algorithm has been tested on synthetic data and real-world datasets, and the results compare favorably to existing robust PCA algorithms. The implementation of the algorithm in Python is also provided. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. By applying this method to the EMO20Q dataset, we enhance the accuracy of its annotations. Furthermore, compared to gold-standard annotations, our findings indicate that annotations produced by human players, guided by this method, are significantly more reliable. This technique's effectiveness is also reflected in the improved performance of machine learning models trained on the revised EMO20Q dataset. We make the revised EMO20Q dataset, along with the annotation-assisted BERT model, openly available to the community.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This would also make it possible to investigate phase transition characteristics of certain materials and provide insights into the unique physics of atomic motion within the Meissner effect's influence. Moreover, this approach could serve as a model for detecting extremely weak fields generated by superconducting quantum interference devices, enabling the precise measurement of small changes in local magnetic fields around quantum systems. The feasibility of this method has been demonstrated in an ideal scenario, and it's anticipated that further advancements in experimental technology will significantly improve the sensitivity even further. The principle behind this method can be applied to detect extremely weak fields generated by other means, making it a valuable approach for the advancement of atomic physics measurement techniques. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming suitable for parallelization on GPUs, characterized by small, uniformly-sized objects with a uniform memory access pattern.  In this context, a parallel memory allocator called DynaSOAr was developed to combine dynamic and static memory allocation techniques, featuring a unique "allocation region" concept that boosts efficiency by minimizing fragmentation and efficient memory packing.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr includes a thread-safe cache that enhances performance by reducing unnecessary memory re-allocation and synchronization costs.  The developed allocator was integrated into the CUDA programming model and extensively tested on a range of applications with object structures.  The results show that DynaSOAr delivers superior performance to both the standard CUDA memory allocator and other advanced, but less efficient, memory allocators like PMR and tbb::cache_allocator, with some applications demonstrating a performance improvement of over 300x.  The research also includes an analysis of the underlying memory access patterns of tested applications, providing insights into the parallelization opportunities of real-world object-oriented programs.  The developed DynaSOAr memory allocator is an open-source tool, available for public use and further development.  In addition, the research includes a freely distributable, lightweight CUDA framework called SOAr-Template, designed to facilitate the easy creation of object-oriented applications with suitable memory access patterns for efficient parallelization on GPUs.  The performance gains achievable with this framework, combined with the DynaSOAr memory allocator, are substantial and were demonstrated in the testing phase.  The research into the underlying memory access patterns of tested applications also led to the development of a tool called SOAr-Inspector, capable of analyzing the memory access patterns of running applications on GPUs.  The tool provides real-time, graphical feedback on the distribution of memory accesses within the SIMD registers of a GPU, as well as the memory allocation patterns of the application.  The insights gained from this research have far-reaching implications for the design of future programming models and memory allocators for SIMD devices, with an emphasis on the underexploited opportunity for efficient, object-oriented programming on these platforms.  The research also includes a discussion of this theme and the associated challenges and solutions.  In conclusion, the development of the DynaSOAr memory allocator has delivered unprecedented performance

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed comparisons were made with experimental data obtained from angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). These comparisons involved an individual manganese adatom as well as two-dimensional manganese dimers on the Nb(110) surface, and yielded insights into the magnetic properties of the YSR states, including their spatial distribution and behavior in response to external electric fields. Furthermore, the theory highlighted the YSR state's dependence on the supercomputer's energy parameters and highlighted the need for accurate measurement of the YSR state's gap in order to fully understand YSR dynamics. Additionally, the theory was applied to YSR states generated by manganese adatoms and dimers on the Ni(111) surface, and safe assumptions were made to extrapolate the results to other transition metal surfaces. The developed theoretical framework has been made publicly available.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system with four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized coin-shaped planet with a temperature that could support liquid water, making it a potential habitable zone. Coin-shaped planets like this one are extremely rare in detections of transiting planets. By measuring the star's brightness, the team determined the planets' orientations in space and found that the Earth-sized planet's orbit is nearly edge-on, while the other planets' orbits are aligned with each other. By analyzing the star's spectrum, the team gathered chemical information about the star, confirming it has a metal content similar to that of the sun. Furthermore, the team estimated the system's structure and found that TOI-712 is a young star with a rotating convective core, surrounded by a massive magnetic field that influences its mass loss rate and atmospheric evolution. The team also calculated the planet's interior compositions and found that the mini-Neptunes likely have thick gas layers surrounding small rocky cores, while the Earth-sized planet's composition is uncertain. The research suggests that the Earth-sized planet's formation was influenced by planetary migration, while the mini-Neptunes may have formed internally with gas giant characteristics. The discovery of TOI-712 highlights the rarity of coin-shaped low-mass planets and the extremely low frequency of planetary systems with multiple transiting planets. The system's youth and the presence of strong magnetic fields and mass loss suggest that the sun was more active in the past, with a higher rate of giant spin-down and mass loss similar to that of the sun. The discovery of a mini-Neptune and Earth-sized coin-shaped planet in the same system presents an opportunity to conduct comparative exoplanetary atmosphere analysis and study the effects of migration and mass loss on planetary formation and evolution. To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a Ti 6-0 and (O, C, N) 5-0 basis set to capture localized bondings between the Ti and the p-doped O or N atoms.  Our results show that both C and N atoms form bonds with the Ti atom, primarily through p-orbitals, but with differing levels of magnetism - likely due to the extra electron in N causing it to behave more similarly to oxygen.  Notably, both defects exhibit a Ti 2p - O 2p hybridization, with N defects displaying a more pronounced effect and possible implications for their influence on nearby energy levels.  Our research also examines the effects of different levels of exchange and correlation functional on the results, ultimately recommending the use of the GPW method to accurately calculate the defects' energy levels.  By analyzing the results, we derived a set of effective Hamiltonians that describe the behavior of these defects and have a clear physical interpretation.  Our findings are consistent with previous experiments and provide a detailed understanding of the N 1s and C 1s near-edge absorption spectra. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted forward of the collider. In traditional top-pair production searches, the focus is solely on the heavy hadronic jets resulting from the decay of top-quarks and W bosons. In contrast, our proposed method utilizes the elastic scattering process of anti-positrons on protons to enhance the sensitivity for low-luminosity datasets. The subsequent identification of forward emitted protons and anti-proton-anti-proton pairs is feasible with the ROMAN magnetic spectrometer or the Semi-Digital TPC in the Muon Spectrometer of the Large Hadron Collider. Our findings indicate ROMAN can detect the top-ratio production cross-section with 3 sigma accuracy at 5.7 fb^-1, whereas the Muon Spectrometer can achieve the same at 10 fb^-1. Furthermore, the proposed measure in ROMAN for calculating the elastic top-quark production cross-section allows deriving the elastic scattering cross-section of anti-top quarks from 28 to 100 fb, based on assumptions regarding the acceptance of the detector for forward emitted particles. Additionally, our research highlights that detecting elastic top-pair production is feasible with the Future Circular Collider, albeit with much lower cross-sections due to reduced elastic scattering cross-sections resulting from the higher energy collisions. The corresponding predictions for the elastic top-pair production cross-section at the Future Circular Collider are 0.157 nb for the ring detector and 0.157 nb for the Roman-Forward, accompanied by detectable rates for forward emitted anti-proton pairs in the Muon Spectrometer of the Large Hadron Collider and 3.4 x 10^9 per second in the Roman-Forward. In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Additionally, we explore a more general approach using a "directed Ramsey theory" equivalent, which enables us to tackle related problems and exciting open research questions. Lastly, we acknowledge that one of the open questions can be solved using a more advanced, recently developed technique.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future with qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. The qudit case also exhibits a greater distinction when comparing the ease of calculating specific operators, with the mass gap being simplest to assess using the massless Dirac operator in the qutrit scenario. The optimal noise threshold for qutrit simulations is found to increase with an increase in qudit dimensionality. The impact of amplitude damping noise is found to have a more significant effect on mass gap calculations when using 9 qudits rather than qutrits. The minimal number of repeated measurements required to reduce statistical noise also decreases with an increase in qudit dimensionality. The research behind this paper is currently unpublished, the original ideas having been discussed with Alexander Korotkov. The key results presented here will likely hold true for other lattice gauge theories that are also hermitian. The noise reduction provided by using qudits instead of qubits can be achieved through the development of better quantum gate implementations rather than classical regression modeling used to calculate mass gap noise. The quantum complexity to calculate the mass gap can be reduced with better implementation of the Dirac operator in particular, and more efficient gauge fermion algorithms in general. The quantum complexity in this context refers to the combination of qudit gate complexity and the necessary amplitude measurements to achieve an accurate mass gap calculation. The findings presented in this paper are specific to sQED but the concepts behind them will likely be applicable to other lattice gauge theories. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the polarization of positrons produced when a highly intense laser is directed at a thin, curved target. The results show that positrons generated in curved targets possess a concentrated "doughnut" polarization pattern outside the focal area, with the maximum polarization reaching over 30% in the middle region. The polarization structure is resistant to changes in target curvature and remains preserved even with increasing electron-positron pair production. The implications of these findings suggest that optimized targets with a focal length could serve as efficient sources for polarized positrons. The necessary target length is found to be directly related to the wavelength of the laser used, with e.g. a 100 micron target length required for a 800 nm laser. The polarization of the positrons also exhibits a linear dependence on the polarization of the initial laser, demonstrating the potential for further enhancement with higher-polarization lasers. The research highlights the capacity for solid-state sources of polarized positrons, with the added benefit of being more cost-effective and harder to degrade compared to gas-based counterparts. The potential applications of these sources in accelerator research, such as the creation of polarized electron-positron pairs or the study of bound state light decay, could be further explored. The findings presented in this study also shed light on the interplay between the geometric curvature of space-time and the spin of electrons and positrons, with the introduced "spin-curvature interaction" term set to be tested by theoretical models. The generated polarization patterns are durable and could be freely propagated, presenting the opportunity to develop schemes for transferring the polarization from the target to other particles through interaction. The study paves the way for the creation of sources for polarized particles through curved targets, with the introduced physics terms set to be applicable across a broad spectrum of high-energy phenomena, from the behavior of electrons in magnetic fields to the interactions of high-energy particles with matter. The potential of solid-state sources for polarized particles in the QED regime could revolutionize the field by providing a solid, and not gas-based, source with lower construction and maintenance costs. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class rank of two. Additionally, it demonstrates that groups with multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup of a specific maximal rank two cannot be defined by a finite set of polynomial equations. This conclusion extends a result by Baumgartner, Breuillard, Tointon, and Wilton. This study also presents an illustrative example of a group that cannot be defined by a finite set of polynomial equations but, on the other hand, is seamlessly integrable within any polynomial diameter group. Consequently, it follows that there are groups with a diameter that scales polynomially which cannot be defined by a finite set of polynomial equations and, as a result, are not solvable.
