This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The temperature sensor was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact footprint of 10{\mu}m x 20{\mu}m. The test results demonstrate its outstanding performance, exceeding the expectations set by prior temperature sensors. The corresponding instruction set and hardware files are available upon request. The design comprises 720 gates, consumes 0.6V to 1.8V, and features a compact size of 10{\mu}m x 20{\mu}m, requiring only 1.06 nJ for each conversion, 10K samples per second sampling rate, a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a $\pm$1.4{\deg}C inaccuracy, and operates within a 0.6V to 1.8V supply voltage range. The operating frequency ranges from 1.6 KHz to 6.4 KHz, enabling it to accurately determine temperatures between -100{\deg}C and 0{\deg}C with a 0.24{\deg}C resolution. The design also includes a simple voltage regulator that can support adaptive voltage scaling. The design was tested across a -40{\deg}C to 85{\deg}C temperature range with a $\pm$1.4{\deg}C inaccuracy, making it suitable for a wide range of applications including automotive systems, industrial devices, and consumer electronics. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores. Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity. We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation. It is proposed that core growth is a critical factor in the formation of high-mass stars, with mass formation efficiency playing a significant role in determining whether low- to intermediate-mass cores will collapse into high-mass stars or lower mass objects. Core growth also offers a possible explanation for the extended birth periods of high-mass protostars. The prevalence of core growth observed in the Dragon dark cloud may have specific geographic expression and further research is needed to assess its universal significance. The phenomenon of core growth has tangible applications for theoretical models of high-mass star formation, such as the core collapse model, by providing a physical timescale for core collapse and suggesting that many high-mass star formation regions are ten times older than previously believed. The associated periods with core masses and mass formation efficiency can influence the mass function of high-mass star formation, offering a potential explanation for the observed prevalence of high-mass star formation. The core growth hypothesis also has implications for the role of gravitational fragmentation and magnetic flumes in high-mass star formation, with predictions made for observable markers of these processes in young high-mass star formation regions. The prevalence of core growth in the Dragon dark cloud stands in contrast to the commonly held view that dense cores are primarily formed through gravitational fragmentation rather than dynamic processes, with the possibility that this view may be an historical artifact of the young sun age of the Taurus star-forming region. The prevalence of core growth may also explain the observed prevalence of low-mass star formation in the Dragon dark cloud, with predictions made for its presence in other dark clouds. The prevalence of core growth may be discerned in the Sagittarius B2 complex, with further research needed to confirm this finding. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the efficacy of one-step recurrences in maintaining (strict) positive definiteness when the space dimension is increased by one. This, in turn, leads to the extension of the Gram series to higher even powers of the distance function. The key challenge now is to tackle the one-step recurrence related to the hyperbolic space dimension. The positive definite nature of the potential tensor product of two zonal functions is explored, which, in turn, enables the determination of the extended space dimension. The analysis also reveals the possibility of extending the space dimension from even to odd when the characterizing system of functions possesses the property of non-negative definiteness. The connection to the MÃmmelsohn matrix and the associated multivariate polynomial is established, which, in turn, leads to the inspection of the hyperbolic space dimension and the associated polynomial roots. The paper delves into the specific example of the hyperbolic space dimension, resulting from the non-negative definiteness of the characterizing system of functions, specifically the tensor product of two zonal functions, namely G_{l,m} and G_{l,n} with l=4. The challenge of determining the hyperbolic space dimension for any given non-negative definite power distance function is posed as an open problem. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of the interfaces. This factor has a significant impact on the distribution of stress and contact angles within the stick-slip regime. The proposed model also provides the characteristic distance over which stress patterns persist. The "leverage rule" and the stationary regimes models can be applied to other non-foaming complex liquids, and our findings have implications for the flow of liquids in narrow channels with rough walls. The appearance of the stick-slip or stationary regimes can be influenced by introducing defects into the foam, which provides an alternative perspective on the slip behavior of smooth interfaces. The prevalence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes has also been linked to the possibility of the creation of grain boundaries within the foam. The roughness-induced friction can be further altered by changing the surface roughness during flow, which has been observed to result in the formation of a granular crystal at the interface. The resulting crystal structure has been characterized and correlated with the contact angle and stress patterns. The formation of a granular crystal can provide an alternative means of controlling the structure of the interface and, in turn, influence the flow of complex liquids. The occurrence of the stick-slip, stationary, or granular crystal regimes has distinct implications for the flow of complex liquids and the behavior of the interface, which can influence the flow by altering the interface structure, creating defects, or shifting to different phases. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. Code for our work is available at github.com/henggao/skin-cancer.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of patterns and the diagram's configuration are determined through a combination of numerical methods that include the application of a spectral stability analysis to evaluate the modal branches' stability. The study also explores both extremely and mildly inextensible scenarios. The results obtained demonstrate that the membrane's inextensibility affects the pattern's development but not the underlying Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability's driving mechanism. The research further reveals that the situation can be approximated by a model that includes both a term representing the curvature of the membrane and a term related to its inextensibility, with the pattern's development being influenced by the inextensibility term's square root. The study also finds that the situation can be distinguished from the analogous two-dimensional situation by examining the relationship between the pattern development and the rate of rotation. The study further examines the extremely inextensible scenario's relationship with the situation where the membrane's tension instead of inextensibility is maximized, with the latter scenario being equivalent to the situation where the membrane's natural curvature is ignored. The study also finds that the situation where the membrane's tension instead of inextensibility is maximized exhibits behavior that is indistinguishable from the extremely elastic scenario that does not include the natural curvature term. Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, with both sets of isomers exhibiting a ratio of abundance for the para and ortho isomers approximately equal to 3. The cloud's kinetic temperature was calculated to be 6.32 K, and the likely formation mechanisms of the detected molecules are discussed. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds are likely formed through magnetic neutral particle surface reactions, whereas the parent compounds may be formed through radical ring closure. The abundance of C (relative to H) in TMC-1 was found to be approximately 1.4 times greater than previously recorded figures, with the abundance of N (relative to H) remaining essentially unchanged. The abundance of the cyclopentadiene and benzene derivatives of CCH and CN is comparable to the abundance of the cyclopentadiene and benzene derivatives of CO. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds exhibit a abundance approximately ten times less than the cyclopentadiene and benzene derivatives of CO. The likely formation mechanisms of the detected molecules are discussed, with the abundance of the cyclopentadiene and benzene derivatives of CCH and CN also discussed in the paper. The paper includes five figures and three tables of data. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/ChenXudongLookAhead/lookahead-tnmt.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. We concluded by highlighting the unique capabilities of J/ψ missing mass distributions in conjunction with other searches for purely invisible decays at e+e- and hadron colliders to provide comprehensive coverage of dark sector physics. Additionally, we offered practical guidelines for conducting effective theory interpretations of J/ψ invisible decays at future facilities. Lastly, we delivered the underlying Mathematica code for likelihood fits used in this study.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the benefits of MFSSA through comparative performance assessments in forecasting and reconstruction tasks. Specifically, we find that MFSSA outperforms MSSA in these assessments. Additionally, our research highlights the optimal parameter settings for real-world applications of MFSSA. Finally, we provide the MFSSA code publicly, available for download.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Finally, by decomposing GCNNs in this manner, we obtain a clearer vision of the underlying principles driving their performance, and potentially opening the path for the invention of more efficient GCNN architectures. A code for the example is available at: https://github.com/ali-ghodrati/GCNN-Matched-Filtering.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. Our approach to designing the structure of logical pseudocodes is deliberate and methodological, starting with a sample algorithm in imperative pseudocode and then transforming it into natural deduction form. This transformation process is accompanied by an executable specification in the form of the Coq proof assistant code. Furthermore, this code serves as a form of proof that validates the algorithm's correctness, providing the benefit of forward reasoning from a premise that is otherwise inaccessible. We also explore the relationship between logical pseudocodes and the natural deduction form in sequent calculus, establishing it as a form of cut admissibility, thereby ensuring the equivalence with the original algorithm specification remains intact. Additionally, this relationship enables us to derive the benefit of efficient proof search through cut elimination, obtaining natural deduction forms from which we can generate logical pseudocodes via cut introduction, in turn obtaining executable algorithms. This in turn suggests that the distinction between imperative algorithms and natural deduction proofs is artificial and based on different perspectives, specifically spatial and temporal ones. We propose the term "algorithmetic formulas" to describe the hybrid structure combining the elements of algorithms and arithmetic formulas, with this structure serving as the fundamental basis for an algorithmetic logic that is capable of capturing both the executable algorithm and the proof of its correctness. We also outline the parameters for a possible formal system of algorithmetic logic along with its associated semantics, including the rules for inference and the semantics for truth, with these parameters enabling the construction of natural deduction formulas from which executable algorithms can be generated, and vice versa. We believe this research opens up the possibility for transforming formal proof systems into executable code, with this transformation obtainable through reverse application of cut elimination, in turn obtainable from the cut admissibility of a given set of natural deduction formulas, with this further implying the equivalence between the original and derived systems, enabling the forward reasoning from premises that were previously inaccessible. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Furthermore, our algorithm delivers an approximate solution with an additive error of $\tilde O(\sqrt{k}\lambda_d(U^T\Sigma V))$ when the initial center set is sufficiently large, and a factor of $k$ improvement when the initial center set is sufficiently small. Notably, when applied to clustering problems defined by a single objective function, our algorithm achieves a guarantee of $O(\sqrt{k}\lambda_d(U^T\Sigma V))$, surpassing the prior storage efficiency boundary while maintaining optimal precision for a broad class of problems, including those with the Frobenius norm objective. We also derive a matching lower bound in the external memory model, validating the optimality of our storage capacity and precision trade-off. Finally, we provide a higher-bound result for the non-amnesiac model, indicating that the storage efficiency boundary can be surpassed with additional reliance on the transient data for problem insight. The algorithm itself is obtained through a combination of our proposed technique, known streaming algorithms, and a suitably selected initial center set, making it possible to execute a 'warm-start' algorithm that efficiently finds an optimal solution for the initial data set. The paper also includes an exploration of a special case, namely the problem of finding the mean of unknown distribution, for which it delivers a storage-efficient algorithm with a guarantee of minimal additive error. Lastly, we and an coauthor previously obtained the main result as well as the generalised case as separate works. The general research problem is also addressed as a part of an larger project examining the impact of additional knowledge on the precision and storage capacity of algorithms. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Additionally, it exhibits the potential to handle significantly larger-scale grid worlds. We term this approach Hierarchical Isolated State Outcomes (HISO). Evaluating HISO on a series of progressively complex grids shows its advantages in terms of computation speed and accuracy in comparison to flat Nash policies. Nevertheless, it falls short in dealing with extremely vast grids. We propose further enhancements to address this limitation, including utilizing a more advanced state definition and incorporating knowledge of the environment's dynamics. These enhancements are demonstrated to yield notable improvements in resolving larger-scale grid worlds. Finally, we outline potential applications of HISO's hierarchical resolution approach to other complex decision-making tasks. Existing hierarchies were cannot be utilized, but it is likely HISO could be grafted onto pre-existing models. Lastly, we highlight the possibility of dynamically updating the individual games with experience, and the potential for HISO to handle multiple pursuing agents. Finally, we outline potential avenues for further research in this area.

Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze the relevance of QCD aperture corrections, electroweak vertex corrections, and radiative corrections in this scenario. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of W and Z particle distribution functions that can be used by event generators, such as MadGraph and Pythia. The development of a Python-based tool called WeZe, which in addition to integrating these distribution functions, also provides event generation through MadGraph, is introduced. The implications of this perspective on 2-to-4 particle interactions in the context of a muon collider are examined. The integration of W and Z particle distribution functions presented in this study can be used by existing event generators, and the inclusion of WeZe provides an alternative event generation method that incorporates near-universal corrections and particle distribution functions, allowing for the generation of events that integrate weak boson collinearity and particle-level final states. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results demonstrate that model-based multi-task reinforcement
learning benefits significantly from modular network designs, allowing for the
efficient learning of distinct tasks without excessive interference. Moreover,
our approach facilitates the seamless transfer to new tasks without requiring

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By integrating these results, we derive some intriguing consequences, including the internal expression of the Godel sentence within any first-order arithmetic system and the impossibility of defining the Peano system using that system itself. Additionally, this integration enables us to prove the undecidability of any formal arithmetic system and highlights the universality of these celebrated results. Lastly, this union also facilitates an examination of the relationship between these theorems and the s so-called "L\"owenheim-Skolem" theorem. The current paper brings together the main arguments presented in those lectures, along with some additional results and the relevant historical context. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, and image deblurring. Because there can be multiple plausible images and the true one isn't known, the primary objective is to sample from the posterior distribution accurately. Machine learning models like Bayesian neural networks provide a straightforward way to access the posterior distribution, but they require a huge amount of training data and aren't often used due to their complexity. A more common approach involves using generative adversarial networks, particularly conditional versions, that can generate new samples from the model's distribution. However, training conditional GANs is challenging due to their instability and slow speed. We propose a new algorithm based on a regularized conditional GAN that generates a distribution similar to the data distribution. This leads to a new objective function that incorporates a term related to the Wasserstein distance between two distributions. We can train this model efficiently using an alternative version of the Earth Mover's distance, specifically the ground pencil penalty, which is computationally inexpensive. One key benefit of this model is that it provides access to the posterior distribution without the need for an inverse transformation, making it suitable for tasks like image generation and clustering. We tested this model on several examples, including restoring degraded images and sampling from the posterior distribution in Bayesian linear regression. The results showed that it generates a distribution similar to the target distribution and compares favorably to other common models used for sampling from the posterior. The model also scales to more complex image generation tasks like MRI reconstruction. The Python code for this model is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghush/RCGAN. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in polynomial systems and the nonexistence of invariant lines in fractional-order systems. Lastly, we discuss the implications of these findings for fractional-order systems with symmetries. The study's results are supported by numerical examples showcasing various system behaviors. The article concludes by highlighting the relationship between fractional-order systems and their equivalent descriptor representations, which may provide further insights into these systems. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, some of which cause the angular broadening and scintillation of pulsars. This Meerkat-LOFAR ASKAP survey reveals significant variability in the angular broadening of the pulsar B1133+16, indicating the presence of multiple screens within one parsec of the Earth. By analyzing the dynamics of this screen, researchers found that one of the screens is moving towards the Earth at a speed of approximately 17.4 km/s and is likely associated with a localized cloud of interstellar gas. Furthermore, the tight polarization of scintillation patterns across B1133+16 suggests that this screen is situated within a localized medium. This discovery highlights the complex nature of the local interstellar medium and underscores the capability of pulsar scintillation to serve as a tool for its in-depth analysis. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Code for Quasi-Periodic WaveNet has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/Parandios/QPNet. Moreover, a pre-trained TTS model based on QPNet for the LJSpeech dataset can be found at: https://github.com/Parandios/ljspeech-tt. Furthermore, the quality of the generated speech in the speech synthesis evaluation also places QPNet atop the list, as demonstrated by the mean opinion score (MOS) results, with a value of 6.522. The model's capacity to adapt to new frequency inputs and unknown signal periods has been proven, with performance comparable to best-in-class TTS models when the input frequency aligns with the training frequency range but significantly better performance when the input frequency differs from the training range. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. All project code and datasets are available for public use.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. The code for LGCN is available at this https://doi.org/10.54489/NVQ34812. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that it can be trained using the widely used Adam optimiser. The findings suggest that LGCN generally performs best when operating in hyperbolic space with a curvature of $4^{-1}$, and it is significantly more effective at balancing homophily and heterophily than existing methods. The intuitive visual representations of the embedded graphs, along with the distinct performance profiles they exhibit, make LGCN a valuable tool for exploring the impact of different geometries on graph classification. The paper also presents an intuitive explanation for the performance enhancements achieved with LGCN. The code for LGCN includes a command to visually visualise the embedded graphs in 3D hyperbolic space. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This novel approach can also be applied to the linearized massive gravitation models of Hassan and Willers or the novel de Rham, Arkani-Hamed, Gubelos, and Karch (dRGAHK) model, allowing for a clear distinction between the five degrees of freedom in the dRGAHK model to arise from choosing a specific de Rham gauge rather than the covariant differential operator alone.  In both cases, adopting an appropriate harmonic or de Rham gauge turns the gauge invariance of the massive gravity theory into the invariance of the full action, thereby facilitating the path integral formulation and providing an explanation for the phenomenon of the absence of the Boulware-Deser ghost in the massive gravity theories.  Furthermore, this note also clarifies the relationship between the harmonic and de Rham gauge theories.  The novel perspective presented here is shown to be compatible with the standard quantization approaches used in the literature.  The introduction of a specific harmonic or de Rham gauge allows for the derivation of the massive gravity field equations from a variational principle, demonstrating that the notion of harmonic or de Rham gauge is not a choice but a fundamental aspect of the massive gravity theories.  The analysis of the scalar fluctuation equation in the dRGAHK model reveals that the harmonic or de Rham gauge is the critical factor in determining whether the model has five degrees of freedom rather than four.  The discussion also highlights the distinction between the covariant and non-covariant harmonic or de Rham gauge, with the former being a choice that results in the five degrees of freedom in the dRGAHK model, in contrast to the four degrees of freedom obtained from the non-covariant gauge.  The novel perspective presented here also allows for the derivation of the massless gravity field equations from a variational principle in the non-covariant harmonic gauge, with the conformally invariant scalar field serving as an example. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a three-level system. We contend that the simplicity of this approach can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, an introduction to the idea of a non-thermal distribution of particles is provided, with an associated visualization. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated.
